This study introduces amended Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integrals and derivatives, which preserve the original formula of the Leibniz rule. By defining a parameter 'p' for integration or differentiation, various cases of the Leibniz rule are derived and proven, including specific instances where 'p' equals 1, yielding the standard integer form of the rule.

This paper analyzes the performance of adaptive filtering methods, specifically those using the least squares method, when identifying the sources of spatially separated signals. We derive the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimate of the signals and establish conditions for their unique identification. Since the LS method minimizes the sum of the squared errors, we examine how it relates to the MMSE estimate and discuss how this connection can be utilized to determine optimal beamformer settings. This framework is then applied to the retrieval of spatially arranged signals, demonstrating its effectiveness.

We've developed an open-source visualization platform called RCSEDv2, which uses web technologies to create interactive views for imaging and spectral data.
The platform consists of multiple tools, including 1D and 2D spectrograms, imaging maps, and continuum/subtraction tools, all built with web components to facilitate customization and integration into web applications.
RCSEDv2 is suitable for a variety of data sources, such as radio astronomy data with velocities along the line of sight, optical spectroscopy with wavelength dependencies, and radio interferometry with spatial dependencies.
The platform is ideal for real-time data analysis, educational purposes, and complex astronomy application development.

Located off the southern coast of Greenland, the Southern Atlantic Ridge exhibits a unique and complex tectonic pattern. Despite being part of the global mid-ocean ridge system, the ridge's geometry doesn't follow the typical symmetrical, azimuthally curved pattern found in other areas of the ridge system. Instead, the Southern Atlantic Ridge features a quadrilinear structure, comprised of the East Greenland Ridge, the Iceland-Faroe Ridge, the Reykjanes Ridge, and the Mohns Ridge. This arrangement of ridges within the region is characterized by highly irregular and interacting plate boundaries, resulting in distinct and varying rates of seafloor spreading. In the present study, we focus on the East Greenland Ridge, where slow seafloor spreading occurs, and used a detailed bathymetric map and sonar data to map the ridge's topography. Our analysis revealed distinct patterns of topographic features along the ridge, including linear mountain ranges, volcanic ridges, and deep troughs, attributed to the movement of tectonic plates over the past 40 million years. The time frame of this analysis was determined using a combination of geological and chronometric methods. The data we collected provides valuable insights into the Southern Atlantic Ridge's kinematics and the complex interaction of tectonic plates within the region, influencing the formation of the mid-ocean ridge system.

As high-resolution medical images become increasingly expensive to obtain, there's growing interest in self-supervised segmentation techniques that utilize only a single image per patient for training. While these methods are cost-effective, optimizing them for poor image quality poses a significant challenge. By redefining the variance-based information objective to account for image boundaries and incorporating a boundary-aware mutual information term, we've developed a multi-scale framework that leverages superpixel representations to enhance the flexibility of information optimization. Our proposed method, characterized by its use of boundary-conscious information and a flexible mutual information term, offers several advantages over existing self-supervised approaches. With lower energy values and higher segmentation accuracy compared to the baseline method, our experimentally evaluated technique demonstrates its effectiveness on the MC-NT2 nucleus segmentation task using the publically available LIOG dataset.

This study proposes a starting point for creating a dungeon master role-playing guide using Artificial Intelligence. The proposed system aims to improve player understanding and guide their actions through the game world. To achieve this, it suggests using a combination of natural language processing techniques, specifically Mind Selection and Intention Recognition. The proposed system consists of two main components. The first component, related to the players' minds, uses clustering and sequence-to-sequence models to create a set of pre-defined intentions linked to specific game elements. The second component, related to the players' intentions, uses a state-transitions approach to update the mind based on the players' actions and the game's state. The proposed system is evaluated using a dataset of Dungeons and Dragons texts, and its effectiveness is compared to a more basic approach using fixed rules. The evaluation shows that the proposed system is more successful at accurately identifying the players' minds and intentions, and the game state, compared to a control group of human dungeon masters. The study also explores the challenges of creating a more realistic game experience with an AI dungeon master.

I've been instructed to notify the forum readers that a new method has been developed for identifying changes in the meaning of words. This method, called LST, uses complex architectures like bidirectional LSTM and GRU to determine variations in the lexical semantics of words over time. In addition, LST was used to create a corpus of semantic changes (CC-Eng) consisting of nearly 4 million word instances with provened semantic shifts, assessed through crowdsourcing and structured queries, in order to evaluate the method's effectiveness. Test results have shown that LST outperforms existing approaches using simple features, particularly on tasks requiring the detection of broad lexical semantic changes. Furthermore, it has been observed that LST performs well on tasks requiring the detection of narrow changes, although it is not consistently better than other methods.

This report delves into the properties of partons as function of the transverse momentum of partons relative to the incoming hadron in the limit of massless particles. It also explores the properties of partons in relation to the movement of hadrons in a parallel direction.

The intricate design of proteins' chemical structures enables their incredible functionality, yet their intricate architecture makes understanding their bending dynamics extremely challenging. To tackle this issue, researchers utilize computational approaches to study protein dynamics, especially those with intricate knots, as these structures are essential for various cellular processes and protein function. Current methods based on computational models excel at simulating global protein movements but often struggle with accuracy when analyzing local features, including bending. This study proposes a novel mathematical concept, called the discrete local crossing number, to identify specific locations on a knotted protein where bending occurs. This approach is independent of the protein's overall shape and can be calculated from space coordinates. To determine the effectiveness of this method, it was applied to a set of knotted proteins, searching for potential bending sites before comparing these predictions to experimental data. The results showed the proposed method's ability to identify bending sites at very low energy levels, demonstrating its potential as a tool for enhancing the accuracy of computational protein modeling.

To resolve the discrepancy between observational constraints and theoretical predictions of structure formation, we analyzed current Planck and BOSS data using a sophisticated statistical method to assess uncertainties, and found additional information to limit the parameters of a Early Dark Energy model. Implementing a novel approach to estimate uncertainties, we found their size to be significantly smaller than previously reported, specifically for the Einstein gravity scenario. As a result, previously accepted solutions to the problem were found to be oversold, and we discovered that the standard Einstein gravity model actually fits the data sufficiently well, even without introducing Early Dark Energy. Furthermore, we found that the data supports the existence of a fraction of dark energy existing very early on, but the parameters of such a component are not well defined, and the existence of a matter-non-conserving interaction between dark and visible matter is also supported, although the rate of such an interaction is not well determined.

Let's consider a symplectic manifold with the standard form, denoted as $\omega$, and a submanifold $V$ that is embedded in $\omega$ with a mapping $f$ that is symplectic and respects the category structure on the blown-up manifold $\hat{\omega}$ and $\hat{V}$. If $V$ has a category structure that is pure of dimension one, we can establish that the mapping $f$ is equivalent to a product mapping $U \times \hat{\omega}_0$ where $U$ is a submanifold of $\hat{\omega}$ with a category structure that is pure of dimension one. If $V$ does not have a category structure that is pure of dimension one, we need to show that the category structure on the blown-up manifold $\hat{V}$ consists of a finite number of projective spaces.

The conventional application of the Jensen's inequality in algebraic scalar field theories has led to an advanced understanding of the irregular Nambu-Goldstone (NG) phenomenon. By utilizing an inequality based on the convex function $\phi(ax+by)$ with $a>0, b>0$ and $a+b=1$, this study generalizes the application of Jensen's inequality to capture the irregular NG phenomenon in quantum field theories including those with spacetime symmetry groups such as the Poincar\'{e} group in the relativistic case and the Galilei group in the nonrelativistic scenario. Additionally, this approach enables the identification of mechanisms driving the irregular NG phenomenon through a convex function analysis. Furthermore, this study also explores the relevance of this phenomenon to theories of quantum gravity within the context of algebraic quantum field theories.

Recent advancements in counterfactual text generation have highlighted the potential of models to create high-quality counterfactuals. However, the current scope of these models is limited, as they primarily focus on individual factoids rather than phrasal relationships. To address this limitation, this paper introduces the concept of counterfactuals in complex sentence structures and proposes a framework called DISCO, which leverages large language models to extract these counterfactuals. Specifically, DISCO incorporates multiple components, including a preprocessor to refine initial candidates and a scorer to evaluate the plausibility of these candidates. To test the effectiveness of DISCO, we introduced the Counterfactual Phrasal Inference Dataset (CPID), a comprehensive dataset consisting of 8000 counterfactual sentence pairs derived from NLP tasks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that DISCO outperforms baseline models and achieves impressive performance on the CPID dataset, demonstrating its potential as a counterfactual generation method. Furthermore, we explored the application of DISCO to real-world scenarios, such as creating counterfactual narratives, and found it to be a valuable tool in this domain.

In this study, we determine the total chromatic numbers along with their community chromatic counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs, namely those based on the powers of a cycle and particular circulant graphs in higher dimensions. By examining these cases, we aim to enhance our understanding of a particular subset of combinatorial optimization problems. The research involves employing both computational tools and theoretical approaches to find optimal solutions for these NP-hard problems. To solve these instances efficiently, we developed a method using a variant of the maximum independent set algorithm and applied it to a broader context. Additionally, we established a connection between the total chromatic number and the maximum degree of a graph, which provides a new fair vertex partitioning ratio. The findings can be viewed from a community structure perspective, where the focus is on identifying special subgroups within complex networks.

The integration of Heusler materials into the semiconductor industry is gaining momentum due to their high spin polarization, which is critical for producing highly reliable magnetic sensors and logic gates. To speed up production, it's essential to develop efficient methods for growing these materials. When it comes to growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on graphene substrates, three possible growth models have been identified: distant epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, and van der Waals epitaxy, depending on factors like temperature and pressure. By understanding these mechanisms, researchers were able to develop techniques to selectively promote or inhibit the formation of defects, which in turn allows for precise control over the electrical properties of the resulting GdPtSb layers.

A new type of code, specifically $p^2$-linear codes, is introduced as a variation of binary error-correcting codes, derived from combinations of subspaces under the action of the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$, with a focus on their isomorphism forms and connections to classical code variants. This research explores the relationship between a $p^2$-linear code's rank and its ability to correct errors, as well as establishing bounds on the number of correctable errors for certain code types. Additionally, this work investigates the connection between $p^2$-linear codes and another type of code, called $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear codes. Slightly more complex, the latter code type is defined using both additive and multiplicative combinations of subspaces, with a specific code, called a $3$-linear code, serving as an example of this category. This research provides several bounds, projections, and duality concepts applicable to these more complex code types.

The flow of viscoelastic fluids through narrow channels is crucial to understanding processes such as polymer injection in oil recovery and extrusion through narrow dies. When a significant amount of pressure is applied, a pressure-driven flow can transition from laminar to turbulent, characterized by the emergence of chaotic patterns in an previously orderly flow. This study, conducted with the aid of stereophotometry, reveals that a specific type of chaotic flow - a varicose instability - can occur even when the flow is not critically balanced and the level of surface tension is moderate. This finding is further supported by numerical simulations using the finite element method. When surface tension is high, a different type of instability - a symmetrical one - dominates the flow. This is attributed to the presence of a stable equilibrium point in the governing equations. These discoveries are also shown to be influenced by the polymer's molecular structure, with better entanglements leading to more unstable flows.

A positive label is typically viewed as a single indicator for a specific class in traditional single-label classification scenarios. In contrast, this paper suggests considering each attribute within a broader classification context that encompasses multi-labels. As a result, the term "instance" becomes a more fitting description than "label". Building upon this foundation, the paper introduces the concept of multi-instance learning where multiple positive instances are used to make classifications across various categories. Due to the difficulty in collecting annotated instances, this paper explores approaches utilizing a single label to gather a set of positive instances, including techniques such as instance-specific activation, aggregation of examples through annotations, and the creation of instance-specific models. Additionally, the paper introduces three challenging benchmark datasets and presents evaluation results for each approach across different data settings, demonstrating the efficacy of using a single label to leverage multiple positive instances. Ultimately, the paper concludes by exploring potential applications of these methods beyond the context of machine learning.

This study explores the energy approach in time-fractional phase-field equations, specifically focusing on the upper bound of energy within the phase-field $\phi$ as time approaches zero. Existing research has established a maximum energy limit $E_0$ via the energy functional associated with the time-ffractional Ginzburg-Landau equation, and this limit determines the upper bound of $\phi$ as time approaches zero. However, the existing upper bound of energy does not apply to all time-fractional Allen-Cahn equations due to the influence of the Caputo and Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives. As time approaches zero, the solution of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with a strong diffusion term under rescaled time and a specific initial condition exhibits a more delicate behavior of the upper bound of energy than that under time-fractional viscosity. As time approaches zero, the energy bound of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with a strong diffusion term can be overestimated by a constant related to $E_0$, and further investigation is required to determine the exact relationship.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and corresponding physical states. This process essentially amounts to taking the underlying mathematical structures and transforming them back into the original physical context from which they were derived. In mathematical terms, this relationship can be expressed as an adjoint pair of functors between two levels of abstract description, with additional properties that reflect key aspects of physicalreality such as the underlying space and symmetry transformations.

The capture of magnetic fields between galaxies results in the formation of narrow beams of gamma-rays, and due to the vast number of these interactions, gamma-rays are significantly more common than expected. By examining the alignment of galaxies' central black holes and surrounding magnetic fields, we can understand the gamma-ray emission patterns. A statistical analysis of nearby galaxies based on their radio waves and black hole characteristics suggests that high-energy gamma-rays are likely caused by the capture of magnetic fields, and that there are likely more gamma-rays undetected due to the limitations of current telescopes. A hypothetical detector with increased sensitivity could potentially detect the powerful gamma-rays associated with these interactions, and offer a more direct path to understanding this phenomenon.

This study examines the variation in portfolio yields across individual investors in an attempt to identify the underlying causes. We test existing theories such as the tax-estate rules, limited capacity, and elassical risk aversion models, as well as a new approach. We gather data from a sample of Canadian households and use it to test the established models, finding them wanting. We then devise a new approach that incorporates a type of mental accounting, which we find effectively explains the dispersion in portfolio yields. This approach can also be utilized to investigate other investment decisions made by these households.

This research paper proposes an advanced method for classifying heart sounds using machine learning techniques. The proposed approach involves using a neural network to classify heart sounds from various sources, including different angles and with added background noise. The researchers tested this method on a dataset containing heart sounds recorded from five different positions and with three types of background noise. They used a large dataset of heart sounds recorded from a single angle for training the model. The results showed that this method can accurately classify heart sounds from different sources and reduce errors due to noise. The model was then tested on a larger dataset of heart sounds recorded from five different positions. The proposed approach has the potential to improve the diagnosis of heart valve disorders using non-invasive methods.

The rising popularity of wearable devices has created substantial opportunities for lifestyle management and healthcare advancement. However, the success of wearable technology lies not only in data collection capabilities, but also in the ability to provide accurate and personalized classification services. A common issue with existing methods is their reliance on high-quality training data, which is often limited by wearers who typically use technology for short periods at a time. To address this challenge, our proposed FedHealth framework leverages federated learning and transfer learning to classify healthcare data from wearable devices without requiring access to raw data. Results show that FedHealth achieves comparable performance to a standard deep learning model using a comprehensive dataset, while significantly outperforming similar methods using a limited dataset.

This study examines various methods used to reduce extreme risks in portfolio theory, focusing particularly on methods based on superior moments portfolio theory. The research highlights the connection between these methods and different parameters of the distribution, as well as the relationship between them. It is shown that minimizing the standard deviation and the skewness of a portfolio is equivalent to maximizing the mean, while correcting for kurtosis involves adjusting for excess kurtosis. The study also explores corrected methods for skewness and kurtosis, establishing a link between these methods and the fourth and sixth moments of returns. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that superization, or the adjustment of moments to match a target distribution, provides a unifying framework for all portfolio theory methods based on moments.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence problem. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field, 
linking it to the universe's inflationary stages through a monodromy charge, thus predicting the 
quintessence's initial minima number to be one less than the number of extra spatial dimensions. 
Even if the universe undergoes several cycle of decompactification and recompactification, 
the charge ensures the quintessence remains dominant in the universe's late stages, resolving 
the coincidence problem.

The success of software-based systems depends heavily on their underlying source code, which also serves as the foundation for various analyses such as vulnerability discovery, performance enhancement, and correct functionality verification. However, handling source code automatically poses significant challenges due to the diverse range of programming languages in use today, with many languages lacking robust parsers and modular handlers. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach called MetaHandle, a high-level handler that can easily be adapted to work with nearly any programming language. By leveraging a generic abstract syntax tree (AST) representation, MetaHandle can seamlessly integrate with withers tailored to each specific language, providing complete support for particular features such as type checking, expression evaluation, and statement execution. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we have developed a prototype based on MetaHandle, which shows that it is possible to handle a wide range of languages such as C, Java, Python, and Ruby with just a few hundred lines of code.

This study explores a complex control issue where costs fluctuate in response to sudden changes, resulting in significantly higher expenses, until the system reaches a stable state, except in rare cases where the costs suddenly spike to infinity. We seek to identify the optimal strategy that minimizes these expenses within a set time frame. Due to the difficulties posed by the model's extreme spikes, we divide the time frame into distinct segments, solving each part separately to create an implicit model of the overall time frame. We establish conditions under which an optimal solution exists and develop a key inequality to estimate the costs during the final segment of the time frame. Interestingly, this inequality reveals the significance of the Berge cyclical monotonicity of the cost function in ensuring the optimal solution is piecewise linear. We also investigate the significance of this property in the context of dynamic pricing, particularly in environments subject to frequency-based discounts.

To resolve outstanding issues in particle physics, like the origin of dark matter and its only present-day interaction with standard model, a leveraged environment is needed. Within a model that incorporates vector leptoquark (LQ) composites, a choice of scalar and pseudoscalar LQs is made to potentially produce these dark matter sectors in hadron collisions. While the production of the two LQs is generally identical, their properties can differ based on their Lorentz nature. In such a case, at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a notable discrepancy exists in the rates at which they are created, with the pseudoscalar LQ produced at a rate about 16% higher than the scalar one. Additionally, this choice of LQ properties offers a need for re-examining existing LHC searches for LQs to ensure they are still applicable. A re-evaluation of these conditions is necessary to ensure current and future LHC searches are effective in discovering the required LQs necessary to solve these fundamental problems in particle physics.

Scientists in life sciences often analyze time series data of limited and varied length, comprising numerous features. The learning process is typically monitored to prevent over-training, given the expensive nature of data relabeling. Despite advancements in deep learning techniques, the life sciences community still lacks broad, high-dimensional time series datasets necessary for effective deployment. The risk of model performance degradation on new data poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, researchers have been utilizing validation sets, but this approach has its own limitations. In contrast, the method presented in this study learns a monitor that assesses the quality of predictions made on new data. This monitor is utilized in conjunction with a predictor to minimize prediction errors on temporal series data. The method is mathematically equivalent to optimal batch learning but offers computational benefits. The algorithm is data-driven, efficient, simple to implement, and effective in handling a broad spectrum of temporal series datasets in the life sciences, as evidenced by results on four diverse datasets. Furthermore, the method is shown to be robust in producing consistent results across multiple random initialization settings. Compared to traditional techniques, it achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced memory requirements. The code for the method presented in this study is publicly available on GitHub.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific cyan lines and three other key properties. We calculated the equivalent width of the lines and found a correlation with gas temperature. Further, we determined that radiation from the Milky Way's center contributes significantly to line flux. This finding is supported by observations of four nearby galaxies. In general, the lines' flux is under-illumined, suggesting that a standard model may not accurately capture galactic conditions. This aspect may be useful in modeling and assessing the standard model's applicability.

We investigate the consequences of combining signal processing irregularties, such as shear smoothing, edge extension, and boundary smoothing, with the compositeness framework, specifically focusing on the impact on angular and edge effects in a particle collision experiment. The analysis applies to various types of experiments, including those at the Large Hadron Collider, and involves interpreting the effects of scalar boson interactions with fermion pairs within a vector boson compositeness framework. The analysis yields more pronounced effects than individual components would, and the optimal observables to study these effects are found to be thrust, kink variables, and edge energies. The increase in edge energies can be as high as 20 GeV in certain scenarios, and the effects mentioned here could be as prominent as 20-50 of the relevant energy scale.

This study explores the reconstruction of sequences from their simplified versions, specifically using the Hamming distance on permutations. We investigate what is achievable with varying lengths of sequences and the method used for their simplification. Our research enables us to establish upper and lower limits for the amount of information required to accurately reconstruct sequences of up to four elements. We have also established theoretical limits for the reconstruction of longer sequences, including those consisting of all unique permutations. Additionally, we investigate the impact of sequence length on the amount of information required, finding that the necessary information grows linearly with sequence length. We have developed two approaches for the reconstruction of sequences, one using all simplifications and the other using only those with the minimum level of detail. We have established the upper and lower limits for the amount of information required to accurately reconstruct sequences of up to four elements for both approaches. We have also established the theoretical limits for the amount of information required for the minimum-level-detail approach in general, finding that twelve bits are sufficient, but we have not yet determined if this is the minimum required.

This note serves as a correction to the paper "A Novel Approach to Learning Musical Instrument Sounds" that was presented at the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing. We are correcting specific claims made in that paper, particularly regarding test metrics and the results of our experiments with the Musical Instrument Recognition (MIR) dataset. These corrections aim to provide a more accurate understanding of the task at hand. Building upon the previous work, we propose developing a protocol that combines dataset-specific training and testing. However, establishing a reliable benchmark for this task proves challenging due to the limited size and diversity of the MIR dataset. Consequently, we suggest using the Dataset-Eval Protocol, which involves using portions of the dataset for both training and testing. This protocol enables the evaluation of several critical aspects of a classification system, including its capacity to recognize novel classes and provide precise class labels. Notably, using the Dataset-Eval Protocol, we were able to achieve a maximum accuracy of 83.75% in recognizing novel classes and an average accuracy of 83.11% across ten trials. Moreover, we observed a maximum accuracy of 82.09% in precise classification and an average accuracy of 80.75% across ten trials. Nonetheless, thoroughly examining alternative techniques such as convolutional neural networks and fixed feature extractors methods was beyond the scope of this study.

Academic researchers frequently rely on Wikipedia as a knowledge source, but often without acknowledging it in their citations. This is evident from an analysis of 5,000 research articles across three disciplines, where Wikipedia usage was detected in over 80% of cases. A study was conducted to understand how these researchers interact with Wikipedia. Over 1,000 Wikipedia entries related to the research articles were identified, and 200 corresponding pairs of research articles and Wikipedia pages were selected for further analysis. These pairs were used to create 200 sets of queries and corresponding Wikipedia responses that provide valuable insights into the nature of these queries. These insights are summarized into eight principles, which can guide the development of subsequent studies utilizing Wikipedia as a source of information. On top of that, a Wikipedia version, called Wikidata, that contains structured data was explored as an alternative to the standard Wikipedia. Finally, the study concludes with recommendations for scholars who intend to build on previous research that incorporates Wikipedia as a source of knowledge.

Modeling merging binary black hole systems using pulsar timing arrays requires consideration of several factors, including the binary's eccentricity and the frequency of gravitational waves. Our research creates a precise method for predicting GWs through a combination of post-Newtonian approximations, and this approach is applied to scenarios involving eccentric binaries. We examine the accuracy and computational efficiency of this method, finding that small uncertainties exist when comparing it to existing models. However, this new method demonstrates significant computational benefits, potentially impacting large-scale data analyses.

We've established precise formulas for the probabilities associated with each possible velocity in the ASEP (Assymmetric Simple Exclusion Process) with N particles on a one-dimensional lattice, especially focusing on the leftmost particle moving to the next site. These formulas, which require knowledge of initial conditions, can be expressed in terms of stationary probabilities that are inherent to the process. Notably, this underlying stationary measure does not need to be exactly the equilibrium measure that typically governs such processes; rather, it may be some skewed variant. Additionally, we've derived explicit formulas for the expected position of the second particle in line with the first one, as well as general expectations for the leftmost particle's position after many steps, including both stationary and transient situations.

This study examines various mathematical frameworks used to model the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and proposes a comprehensive SEIRPHM model. The model's structure is based on a fundamental framework that incorporates a detailed description of human physiology and incorporates the effects of physical distancing measures. The model's parameters are estimated using real-world data from the Epicov study. A numerical analysis of the model is conducted to explore the dynamics of the epidemic under different physical distancing scenarios. Specifically, the model is used to investigate the impact of increasing physical distancing on epidemic peak time, final epidemic equilibrium, and latent infection period. The study also examines the conditions under which the model exhibits oscillatory behavior and provides analytical solutions for specific physical distancing levels. The study's findings are validated using numerical methods and the model is applied to derive policy recommendations for controlling the epidemic peak and reducing the infection period. The study's viewpoint is presented from a single perspective and the study's results are unique. The study's approach may be of interest to researchers in the field of applied mathematics and epidemiology.

The paper explores the unique properties of a Majorana particle, specifically examining its distribution function and the implications for the particle's charge conjugation symmetry. It also derives the necessary conditions for the particle's existence, including constraints on its distribution and the average 4-momentum. The study assumes a Majorana particle moves at relativistic speeds and is described by the Dirac equation, with the goal of understanding the relevance of CPT transformation. The CPT symmetry is found to be satisfied for an arbitrary distribution of such particles. The study also investigates the consequences of linear polarization and provides Lorentz invariance conditions for the particle's four-dimensional distribution characteristics. It is demonstrated that the charge conjugation symmetry can only hold if the distribution function is isolated to a specific frame of reference. The study further reveals that linear polarization necessarily violates the charge conjugation symmetry, implying that a Majorana particle with a linear polarization distribution cannot satisfy CPT symmetry.

Communicating online incurs a significant loss in contextual cues, such as tone and language nuances, leading to misinterpretations of abbreviations and acronyms. To better comprehend user intentions, a system has been developed to identify and explain the meaning of abbreviations in user-generated content, thereby enhancing user interaction and system performance. To achieve this, a rule-based approach has been employed, combining syntactic analysis with a pre-defined set of rules to accurately determine the structure of the user's input, followed by the retrieval of the desired acronym definition. To facilitate testing and improvement, a web-based platform has been developed, allowing users to submit examples along with desired outcomes, thereby enabling the exploration of alternative detection methods and providing a means for system optimization.

The interplay between atom-dimer interactions and spinor symmetry has unique effects in certain systems, offering potential control over atom-dimer conversion rates. We investigate the process by which a spin-polarized triplet atom interacts with two superfluid fermion atoms, leading to the formation of a spinor dimer and providing a means to influence its formation via light-matter interaction. A model is presented that includes two variations: in the first, we consider the impact of applied light on a process with coupled atomic states, resulting in the formation of a dimer in a certain spin state; in the second, we examine the effect of light on a process with decoupled atomic states, leading to the creation of a dimer in another spin state. This second process is more susceptible to light-induced interference, offering a means to regulate the conversion rate.

This study introduces an improved method for updating hierarchical data in DNA storage, incorporating error correction and a new binary tree storage structure. The proposed update assistance scheme divides data into mutable and immutable parts, allowing for efficient retrieval and rewriting of specific information without affecting the entire database. Computational simulations demonstrate that this technique surpasses the previous method's performance in update speed, storage requirement, and error correction capability.

Topological insulators exhibit unique properties where exceptional points in energy spectrum form lines or surfaces, separating distinct conjugate modes. These nodal surfaces play a crucial role in the unique physics observed in topological systems. The Weyl points that nodal surfaces connect can be linked to understand the system's bulk and boundary physics. Recent advancements in nanophotonics and other fields have made it possible to experimentally realize and study nodal surfaces in various topological phononic systems, revealing potential applications including robust propagation of modes and enhanced optical responses.

A complex procedure requires accurate differentiation and marking of tumors, particularly neuroblastic tumors, for effective treatment planning.  We have introduced MAG-Net, a directed multilayer network that efficiently identifies and classifies brain tumors by effectively utilizing expert-derived segmentation guidelines.  We have also proposed a novel approach to direct the network's focus on specific regions, leveraging spatial relationships between tumors and anatomical structures to achieve this.  To train the model, we have utilized a relatively small dataset consisting of MRI images, and evaluated its performance against a larger set of unseen images, demonstrating its generalization capabilities and competitive results compared to other leading methods.

Differentiating shadows mathematically has been challenging, leading to limitations in computational methods, especially those employing differentiation techniques such as gradient-based optimization. This paper introduces a novel approach to accurately calculate cast shadows, applicable to both external and internal shadow scenarios, even in complex situations involving polygonal objects with arbitrary orientation. This approach has the benefit of being differentiable, enabling its use in solving inverse problems related to light and material properties in the presence of shadows. The paper also presents specific algorithms for differentiating the shadow function, which has been shown to be effective in problems involving shape, light, and material identification in images affected by shadows. This research paves the way for the effective use of optimization and machine learning techniques in solving inverse problems in computer vision and computer graphics.

Due to the prevalence of cost-effective and high-quality smartphone cameras, users are increasingly capturing and sharing video content, particularly on social media, from potentially moving cameras with interlaced formats. To address this common issue, researchers are working on developing effective deinterlacing techniques. Presently available methods primarily apply before-and-after frame extrapolation, yet these typically yield underwhelming results when confronted with rapidly moving video sequences. To overcome this challenge, this study proposes a novel deep learning-based deinterlacing technique, tailored for real-time video processing, by incorporating a spatially varying deformation field. The proposed network architecture is computationally efficient and simple to implement. The research team evaluated their method against conventional techniques and other deep learning-based approaches using two extensive datasets of real-world video footage, capturing its applicability to still images and video sequences affected by camera shake, resulting in remarkable PSNR and SSIM performance improvements.

We investigated the semantic difference between the average square radius of the neutron point spread, also denoted as $\langle r^2 \rangle$, as calculated using the relativistic mean field model and its non-relativistic counterpart. Our analysis revealed that $\langle r^2 \rangle$ differs significantly, with the choice of theory influencing the result by a factor of up to two. This discrepancy arises essentially from the varying density distributions observed in nuclear matter when calculated through the two methods. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that the neutron density in nuclear matter behaves dissimilarly in relativistic and non-relativistic frameworks, with the former exhibiting a more contracted density profile and the latter a super-dense core. These distinct density profiles, in turn, lead to distinct predictions for the electromagnetic form factor in momentum space. Interestingly, the difference in $\langle r^2 \rangle$ is not solely a relativistic effect, as the non-relativistic models including the well-known Sharma-Ma fontaine model also yield a value of approximately 16 fm^2, very close to that obtained from the relativistic mean field model.

We have designed a deep learning-based method that surpasses traditional solvers in solving the shallow water equations, while also exhibiting potential benefits for real-world applications. By leveraging deep learning, our method can solve the shallow water equations from scratch in a matter of milliseconds, even with large inputs, whereas typical linearized solvers take significantly longer. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by comparing its performance to established solvers in numerical experiments, revealing that our method outperforms the alternatives in terms of execution speed. Additionally, we have explored the application of our method to the solution of partial differential equations with time-varying boundaries by utilizing the boundary identification problem as a precursor step.

HDR photography combines three pictures taken at varying exposure levels to
contrasting ones to achieve a photo with a wider dynamic range. This process can
be semi-automatically carried out using smartphone apps, yet these methods are
limited by the slow time gap between consecutive photos, causing issues with
capturing moving subjects. A new method proposes using a single algorithm to
simultaneously control the camera's exposure and take two photos with different
exposure settings, followed by a fusion technique to create a final HDR image.
The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experimental data,
showing it can be up to 10 times faster than traditional techniques while
producing comparable results. Furthermore, the method is capable of handling moving
subjects, and testing on a variety of scenes validates its applicability to
everyday photography scenarios.

Our research aims to address the unresolved challenge of quantifying model performance uncertainty in neural networks, particularly when used with partial and deliberately distorted data for training. By leveraging causal entropy, our approach develops effective methods to measure and manage uncertainty during training, ensuring optimal generalization capabilities. We evaluate these techniques through simulations and real-world experiments, finding they outperform current state-of-the-art methods and demonstrating the significance of considering both data quality and labeling costs in the optimal training process. Our optimal policy is efficient, readable, and easy to understand due to its transparent parameters compared to other neural network training policies. Moreover, our approach is relevant to broader machine learning questions, such as the relationship between data, models, and generalization.

Achieving uniform heating throughout a solid particle bed is critical for enhancing gas-phase reaction rates. Although numerous methods exist for heating such beds, their temperature distributions remain poorly understood, especially in cases where the particles transition from loose to compactly packed. Utilizing rapid MRI, our study provides the first direct observation of temperature distributions within stationary gas-solid beds subjected to electric heating, revealing significant variations influenced by particle size and the presence of moisture. Interestingly, lower water content appeared to increase temperature non-uniformity before it was mitigated by further increases.

This note provides an updated proof of the conjectured result from "The b-principle for trees" that certain combinations of submersions with trivial normal bundles can be found, given a specific condition is met. Specifically, if a set of differentiable manifolds can be divided into two groups such that the manifolds in each group have a specific property in common, then it should also be possible to divide the set into three groups such that the manifolds in each group share the same property. The updated proof involves a simpler demonstration of a crucial theorem.

The meso-scale mechanical behavior of heart tissue during fibrillation is governed by a system consisting of three components: an electromechanical feedback loop, tissue structure, and biological material properties. Due to the highly disordered and complex nature of heart tissue, a 3D representation is not feasible for computational simulations, so a more manageable multilevel structure representing tissue histology has been adopted by multiple researchers. 

Several researchers have used the term "meso-scales" to describe structural arrangements at the level of individual muscle cells, but there is a lack of standardization in terms of spatial extent and definition across the literature.

Our study compares three distinct definitions of the muscular tissue mescoscale, ranging from very fine (defined as the intracellular level) to much coarser definitions, in order to determine their impact on computational simulations of cardiac mechanics.

The three definitions are as follows:

*   $${\text{L}}_{{{\text{meso}}_{\text{med}}}} = 200\,\upmu \text{m}$$, representing the length of muscle cells before stretching, referred to as the medium-scale.

The study considers a matrix model with independent and identically distributed entries, specifically semi-circular elements, under the constraint that the upper triangular entries form a non-decreasing sequence. Based on an underlying process involving non-decreasing partitions, the theorem establishes the limiting characteristics of the empirical spectral distribution for an associated Hermitian matrix. Furthermore, the result applies across various settings, including both finite and infinite size matrices, as well as scenarios involving distinct distributional assumptions for matrix entries. The method employs an innovative approach, combining elements of an earlier proof along with new techniques to extend the validity to a broader class of distributional assumptions. The associated test function theorem proves an essential result for the theorem, itself a significant achievement in the field.

The emergence of cutting-edge AI techniques in video creation has been a significant shift in technology, allowing for the development of innovative applications such as video editing and manipulation. This has sparked growing interest in various research communities, leading to an explosion of studies on video modification using deep learning. To provide a clear overview of this rapidly evolving field, we have conducted a comprehensive survey encompassing not only the most notable studies but also extracting essential insights on the underlying concepts, techniques, and challenges. This survey is organized around three central topics: artificial intelligence-based video manipulation, analysis of temporal changes using deep learning, and AI-driven video creation from scratch. This review is a valuable resource for researchers seeking to explore the complexities of AI-driven video creation and offers a foundation for future breakthroughs in this emerging field.

Users of DVP-based models, who make decisions independently of the model's predictions, can still be influenced by the model's perceived reliability. This is demonstrated by analyzing the distortion created by manipulating adversarial attacks, which incorrectly authenticates user-generated images. It is shown that these attacks can mislead users into a false sense of security, as the attacks' impact on the classification decision varies significantly, depending on the image content. Moreover, we find that high-quality manipulations are more likely to go undetected by both human eyes and automated detection systems. In addition, we find that these attacks not only affect the classification outcome but also the confidence level of the classification, which is a critical aspect of the system's robustness. To address this vulnerability, we propose a new, more robust approach that incorporates a diverse set of classification models and evaluates their individual reliability. This proposed approach is effective in mitigating the false sense of security caused by manipulations, which could have practical applications given the prevalence of deep learning-based classification systems in everyday life.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for advanced acoustic imaging and anomaly detection applications. We investigate the concept of ultra-high frequency microacoustic metagratings utilizing two-photon lithography, which could potentially integrate complex nanostructures for enhanced sensitivity. To overcome fabrication limitations, we simulate space-f filter-like microacoustic metagratings at very high frequencies, demonstrating the potential for massive surface area enhancement and localized anomaly detection. However, the f filter's efficiency significantly declines with increasing frequency, a challenge that future research aims to address.

This study uncovers the underlying random nature of spatial variability to drive anomalous non-normal diffusion. We demonstrate through mathematical modeling that diffusion con be described by a family of fractional in time and space equations, resulting from the random distribution of water flow's permeability within a given area. Our approach involves establishing statistical relationships between spatially distributed fractions of time derivative and integral operators, ultimately leading to the parameter estimation necessary for fractional diffusion models. By applying this approach to empirical data, we show that traditional approaches fail to capture the complexity of the data, leading to an application of our method to a numerical solution method.

A comprehensive model is presented, capable of simulating both linear and nonlinear interactions between modes in optical resonators and waveguides. The model encompasses a broad range of geometrical configurations, including circular symmetry, general elliptical shapes, and rectangular shapes. It provides accurate calculations for field distributions, electromagnetic energy patterns, and mode coupling coefficients in linear optical systems. When applied to systems with Kerr nonlinearity, the model can simulate linear and nonlinear interactions, including mode coupling, phase modulation, and the formation of optical solitons.

In systems controlled through continuous variables under no constraints, a control objective is achieved if there exists a negative-definite function that satisfies specific properties in relation to the system's dynamics and controls. This paper builds upon a previously established converse theorem for a broad class of systems described by differential equations, by demonstrating that a suitable Lyapunov function can be obtained in conjunction with a conversational steady-state controller. Additionally, the paper is adapted to apply to regulation systems with control constraints, and subsequently, to systems represented by differential inclusions and switching systems. The developed techniques also yield insights into the robustness of the specified control properties.

This research paper proposes a novel deep learning approach, utilizing generative adversarial networks, to enhance low-resolution flow velocity images and estimate turbulent flow velocities at higher resolutions, potentially expanding its application across various Reynolds numbers.

This paper formulates mathematical inequalities based on the wave equation, applicable to obtaining bounds in models of scattering theory, particularly in formulating estimates for the semigroup generated by a specific self-adjoint operator.

Customizable automotive systems rely on ISASPs to ensure safety and effectiveness, but relying solely on pre-programmed rules may not account for the complexity of real-world driving scenarios. While learning-based approaches can handle these situations well, the issue of open-world ambiguity remains, as there may be an infinite number of possible scenarios. Our novel framework addresses this challenge by dividing the learning process into two parts: first, the ISASPs learn about the underlying rules that apply to a specific set of scenarios, and then they use these rules to infer what principles likely hold in new situations. Our approach enables the efficient handling of an infinite number of possible scenarios by leveraging a small number of examples to learn about the underlying patterns, and our results show that it outperforms a random forest baseline in a simulation test.

Continuous reinforcement learning scenarios pose significant challenges in evaluating learning agents due to their ever-changing nature, making traditional fixed episodic evaluation methods less effective. This issue is particularly pronounced in applications involving multiple parallel agents, such as games with multiple players or dynamic grids with multiple agents. To address this limitation, this evaluation framework introduces several key innovations, including dynamic episodic fragmentation, a score aggregation method called episodic mean diagonal length, and a parallelized episodic processing technique. This evaluation framework is highly versatile, supporting a wide range of continuous reinforcement learning tests, including but not limited to, multi-player games like Hanabi and Asymmetric Coordinated Strike, as well as complex grid worlds resembling a diverse range of cities. This evaluation framework is an open-source project available on GitHub, offering numerous benefits to researchers, including enhanced transparency, reproducibility, and a user-friendly interface for customizing evaluations.

Declative process mining focuses on discovering underlying processes responsible for specific outcomes, without regard for time or other details. As processes evolve over time, it's essential to update our understanding of the processes. This paper introduces a method for monitoring and updating declative processes as new data becomes available, allowing for notifications based on changing process patterns. The approach leverages real-time data and declative queries to effectively monitor processes for deviations, sending alert streams in the process. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a real-world application and a comparative evaluation of its performance with existing techniques.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden localization transition as quasiperiodicity is altered. Our study reveals that in a one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal array, light localization can shift to a more distant quasiperiodic configuration, a phenomenon we term reentrant delocalization. This unusual occurrence is made possible by combining numerical simulations and an analytical model, which allows us to navigate the transition between localized and extended states. According to our analysis, the reentrant delocalization shift results from the interplay between two competing influences: a immediate localization mechanism driven by the quasiperiodic structure, and a delayed delocalization mechanism involving an extended state emerging from the quasiperiodic structure's margin.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Mauna Kea Infrared Test Camera to test its sensing capabilities. To prepare for this test, we designed an experimental data acquisition system using a field-programmable gate array and a high-speed camera link. However, this approach was later altered due to technical difficulties, and we implemented an alternative data processing system based on a direct memory access technique. Additionally, we established connections between Liger and the Mauna Kea Infrared Test Camera using various software frameworks, and we present the data processing system we developed for the tests.

Optical systems are increasingly dependent on the spatial mode demultiplexing capability, which allows for the separation of independent information channels. While traditional approaches based on beam splitters and interferometers are effective, they can also limit the system's capacity due to limited resolution. A novel method involves the application of the quantum principle of multiphoton entanglement to achieve spatial mode demultiplexing. Although this technique shows great promise, the method faces a significant challenge in practice - the limited resolution of the system is severely restricted by the uncertainty principle by a factor of sqrt(2) over traditional methods. A novel approach is proposed, based on the application of a quantum transformation to the incoming field, which can increase the resolution by a factor of 2 when certain sources are used. Furthermore, we show that this technique can achieve super-resolution, overcoming the restriction imposed by the uncertainty principle, potentially enabling a significant improvement in optical communication capacity.

This study proposes novel algebraic and analytical constructs to define the spaces in which scalar field theories are parameterized, specifically for SYK and multi-QYB models, using beta functions as their boundaries. For the S^d beta function, we establish an algebraic representation of the space as the projective variety defined by the beta function and its derivatives, and we show that this definition is equivalent to the analytical construct defined by the stochastic quantum gravity flow equation. This definition enables us to examine the properties of the space, including its singularities and mirror symmetry. Notably, we find that the space has multiple copies of the hypersurface where the beta function's derivative vanishes, and it has an algebraic definition that corresponds to the point where the imaginary part of the conformal time period changes sign. We also find that the space has a symmetry under the transformation that exchanges the couplings and the imaginary part of the conformal time period. For the beta function of the SYBQ model, we propose that the space has an algebraic definition as the variety defined by the supergravity beta function and its derivatives, and we show that this definition is equivalent to the analytical construct defined by the honeybee flow equation. This definition enables us to examine the properties of the space, including its singularities and mirror symmetry. We're investigating a dynamic ecosystem composed of two demographic groups, where we measure their interaction rates based on age and other factors. However, the challenge lies in predicting significant population shifts due to the intricate relationship between their age structures. Our research focuses on identifying early warning signs and lasting changes in the ecosystem's transition. We've developed a comprehensive analysis of the ecosystem's response to changes, involving a detailed examination of the transition process, the impact of the rate of change, and the influence of the ecosystem's initial state. Furthermore, we've established a set of indicators that can detect significant changes, and our approach is adaptable to different contexts, making it a valuable tool for predicting lasting changes in demographic shifts.

A multitude of studies has investigated the correlation between star formation rates and gas masses in galaxies, yet there has been a notable lack of consensus regarding the role of major mergers in shaping this relationship. Our research involves a vast sample of $3.8$ million galaxies for which we have morphological and spectral observations. We employ machine learning algorithms to classify galaxies based on their morphological features and detect those with distinct bulge components, before separating them into merger candidates and control groups. The results of our study reveal that massive bulge hosts, especially those undergoing major mergers, follow a different star formation mass sequence. These galaxies' massive size and early stellar population suggest they have ancient bulge components that formed through major mergers. Furthermore, our findings indicate that massive bulge hosts that have undergone major mergers populate the high-mass extremities of the star formation mass sequence, while their non-merging counterparts occupy the low-mass extremities. This implies that massive bulge hosts represent a distinct population that turns over in the star formation mass sequence due to their unique history of major mergers.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across different languages, leveraging high-performance neural multi-task models. Given that numerous prior studies have focused on sentiment datasets native to specific languages, we employed neural network-based models suitable for low-resource language sentiment analysis, incorporating datasets from other languages to facilitate cross-language learning. The underlying code and results indicate that sharing knowledge across languages can yield remarkable outcomes, with the benefit of using English datasets visible in languages without further training. The proposed approach provides a practical solution for addressing sentiment analysis challenges in low-resource languages.

Humans exhibit a unique capacity for self-criticism, often arriving at accurate diagnoses of their own errors. Yet, an excessive preoccupation with flaws can be detrimental. To capture this duality, we introduce a theoretical model where individuals are capable of reviewing and revising their own work. Our analysis reveals that, given sufficient time and resources, humans can balance self-criticism with the need to complete tasks efficiently. We support these findings with data from an online experiment involving a similar task. The results show that, when given the opportunity, humans can benefit from self-criticism, and this advantage is particularly pronounced in contexts where they have some control over the outcome. We also uncover additional insights from our data, including the observed phenomena that men generally participate in the study at a lower rate than women and that the most skilled participants tend to be more self-critical.

In 1991, Gary Freiman proposed a conjecture known as the 3k-4 conjecture, which is an enhanced version of the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsen theorem. This conjecture remains unsolved, and many variations including the sum-set conjecture can be derived from it. We have successfully demonstrated a more robust form of the 3k-4 conjecture, specifically for sets contained within a specific structure, namely those with a large number of elements (k >= 100), allowing us to establish new proof for certain cases of the sum-set conjecture, the Fugleberg-Katznelson-Rosenbaum theorem, and a modified version of the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsen theorem.

The Fourier transform plays a key role in understanding the properties of fractional Brownian motion's characteristic function. By analyzing this transform, researchers have established conditions to identify the local geometry and global distribution of fractional Brownian motion's parabolic surfaces within Euclidean space. Specifically, they have determined the volume and interior structure of these surfaces based on the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. While previous studies have provided insights into the geometry of these surfaces, further analysis is needed to gain a deeper understanding of their topological properties. In the case of fractional Brownian motion with positive drift, the surfaces' geometry is well understood, but the condition $\beta=0$ requires a different approach. By examining the Fourier transform of the characteristic function, researchers can establish conditions to identify the local and global geometry of parabolic surfaces, but these conditions are more complex and involve an infinite series. Although the condition is complex, it does provide a clearer understanding of the geometry of these surfaces, but it is unclear if it is biologically relevant.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, a H\'enon-Heiles potential is modified to create a simpler, quasi-classical model. The trial wavefunction chosen has two parameters, with one being related to a harmonic oscillator in three-dimensional space, and the other acting like an angular momentum operator for spinless particles. Calculations to determine energy and disorder are performed within the Jackiw-Kerman framework, showing that the H\'enon-Heiles system exhibits quantum disorder. Results are analyzed at different potential energy ratios, and variations in energy and disorder are explained through H\'enon-Heils's momentum-dependent potential.

X-ray images contain subtle details that can aid in predicting severe cases of COVID-19.  A patient's condition can be critical only if it is life-threatening, as defined by the WHO.  Therefore, the objective of this study is to develop a model that can accurately identify life-threatening cases of COVID-19 from X-ray images.  The proposed system consists of two components: a classification model to determine critical COVID-19 cases and a secondary model for patients tested positive for COVID-19.  The model is known as the Critical COVID-19 Baseline Model.  To verify the effectiveness of this system, an experiment was conducted using the MIMIC-CXR8 dataset, which is a publicly accessible dataset containing chest X-ray images and patient data.  The evaluation was performed on a subset of the dataset, and the results showed that the proposed model outperformed the existing benchmark model, achieving a 95.8% accuracy rate for detecting severe COVID-19 cases.

The global simplicial bundle constructed in a categorical framework based on the Dold-Kan correspondence can be interpreted as a natural simplicial structure. This interpretation applies particularly to categories like simplicial categories and categories of simplicial objects, and even allows the concept of global simplicial bundle to be seen as a generalization of the simplicial functor that constructs the universal bundle.

The incorrect matches in visual association retrieval pose a significant challenge, as they diminish the effectiveness of models in identifying accurate connections between images. The sheer scale of potential associations makes traditional methods of incorrect suppression unfeasible. In contrast, leveraging a mixture model of foreground and background probabilities proves insufficient in isolating the desired target. In this research, we propose an alternative method that focuses on the complemental approach - identifying the areas likely to contain an incorrect target instead of the correct one. This method is grounded in a mixture model where the background category holds a significantly higher probability than the foreground. We introduce a straightforward yet highly efficient technique for training a network to minimize the incorrect matches by reducing the probability of the background category. This technique enables a significant reduction in errors at a modest increase in computational cost. Our results demonstrate that this method yields substantial improvements in accuracy on the VGGFlow dataset, with an error reduction of 12.8% when using a pre-trained network and 14.6% when using a trained network.

This study proposes a new sampling technique called Delta Sampling for action recognition challenges that are constrained by limited data. Due to the constraint of using a small amount of video per clip, recent successes in action recognition cannot be directly applied, especially when the dataset is heavily dependent on additional information from surrounding clips. Delta Sampling addresses this issue by focusing on the most distinguishing features of videos by leveraging a BERT-based model. Furthermore, to enhance the performance of data with poor lighting, the study incorporates additional data with natural lighting and modifies the training process to give more importance to low-light videos. The proposed technique, including delta sampling and the improved data preparation process, is tested on the EpicKitchen-52k dataset and shows superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a novel concept called Content Addressable Concurrent Processors, a pioneering technology that allows multiple instruction streams to be simultaneously executed on a single core, leveraging content-addressable memory for both data lookup and re-routing purposes. By integrating this technology into a FPGA, we achieved a 2.5 times performance enhancement in benchmark tests compared to a standard processor, and additionally, our(Content Addressable Concurrent Processors) design exhibits 10 times lower energy consumption than a typical CPU during specific operations.

We perform an in-depth analysis of massive, distant galaxy clusters to better understand the formation and development of disk galaxies during the early universe. By examining a $z=2.91$ galaxy cluster containing 20+ galaxy members within a $k$-band magnitude range of $M_k=-20.3$ to $-17.7$, we obtained high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy and high-resolution optical-to-submillimeter imaging. Our data set includes observations from $0.12~\mu$m to $1.5~$mm, enabling a comprehensive analysis of galaxy star formation, gas accretion, and potential major mergers. By examining rest-frame far-infrared to submillimeter emission, we discovered that all galaxies within the cluster are engaged in star formation, with rates ranging from $1.6~\rm{L}_* (M_k>-19.5)$ to $60~\rm{L}_* (M_k+19.5)$. Furthermore, we observed star formation rates that were twice as high in galaxy cores than in outer regions. By examining gas content and gas accretion streams, we found that all galaxies within the cluster are being supplied with gas at typical cosmological rates, with about half the galaxies being fed by gas streams. Our observations indicate that galaxies within the cluster exhibit distinct structural components, including disk regions that are substantial ($1.7 \pm 0.3$ times the size of their stellar bulges

A widely accepted theoretical concept in the Texture Zero of Flavor (TZF) model is being challenged in this study. Based on a comprehensive and systematic analysis, researchers have developed an automated algorithm to automatically generate the complex Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix. This method is highly efficient, enabling a thorough exploration of the TFZ parameter space by eliminating the need for manual matrix construction. Upon examination, the theoretical Cabibbo angle was found to be inconsistent with experimental measurements, a discrepancy that cannot be resolved within the confines of the TFZ framework. As a result, the model is unable to accurately predict key observables such as the CKM matrix's Jarlskog invariant and the unitarity constraint, both of which lie outside the TFZ's prediction range. Despite over-reliance on semi-analytical expansions that limit its global reach, this study demonstrates the capability of a robust Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to accurately determine the global minimum of the TFZ function. This capability enables the exploration of the TFZ parameter space in a more comprehensive manner, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the TFZ's underlying structure. Allowance can be made for a certain degree of numerical imprecision in the minimum energy value, nonetheless a crucial constraint of the TFZ, namely that it operates within a global minimum, remains intact.

This research paper addresses specific solution types, presences, local characteristics and periodic behavior for a particular class of elliptic equations. It provides conditions under which solutions exhibit periodic characteristics in both one and higher-dimensional spaces. It also establishes criteria for distinguishing between solutions that are both present and local minimums. It demonstrates that certain solutions which are presence and local minimums can be classified into different categories based on their characteristics in one-dimensional space. It also provides conditions under which solutions that are presence, local minimums and periodic in one-dimensional space can be classified into different categories in multi-dimensional space. It provides a minimum and maximum value for the given Bubbling tree. It also provides a 9-element set that includes all possible presence and local minimum solutions in one-dimensional space. It provides a 12-element set that includes all possible presence and local minimum solutions in two-dimensional space. It provides a 15-element set that includes all possible presence and local minimum solutions in three-dimensional space.
