Despite the importance of this issue, existing approaches to detecting false news are not entirely effective and often lack a solid understanding of the underlying language structures. This paper introduces an innovative method that combines advanced language techniques to automatically identify and exclude irrelevant information from extended text samples, including long news articles. By condensing these articles into essential summaries, our method enables the effective comparison of text to an established gold standard set using existing classification techniques. Our experimental results demonstrate that condensing text via our proposed approach significantly enhances the accuracy of false news identification.

This investigation focuses on the impact of curvature in Gaussian random fields on their associated stationary processes, which can be achieved through transformations of their parameters. By exploring how Gaussian random fields behave under linear transformations, particularly on plane domains with varying curvature, this study aims to understand how Gaussian processes are affected when their indices are altered, which is a significant question in mathematics. To this end, this study establishes relationships, finds conditions for consistency, and examines how changing the index affects the asymptotic behavior of extreme value quantities such as the supremum's distribution, the excess over a high threshold, and the tail of the survival probability.

This research paper proposes a new concept called Secure Nested Opportunistic Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access, or SefcNOIMA for short. It aims to address the current limitations of NOMA by providing a solution to the "hyperpower" problem and offering better protection to weakly connected users. Based on a new encoding technique called "differential encoding," SefcNOIMA enables a trusted encoder to convey a confidential message to an untrusted receiver while protecting the secrecy of the original message. A 1-bit feedback system from the receiver to the encoder facilitates this process. To evaluate the performance of SefcNOIMA, the paper derives an expression for the minimum entropy of the noise at the receiver and investigates the optimal distribution of power between two users. Additionally, the paper shows that a 50/50 power allocation maximizes the minimum entropy of the noise, leading to a secure connection for both users. Furthermore, the paper explores the scenario of single-antenna transmission and provides a 90% secrecy rate achievement condition for two users. The research findings can be applied to various applications, including wireless networks and multi-user systems.

We have developed an iterative algorithm to calculate the principal component associated with the $\ell_1$-norm for a specific type of data set that exhibits rotational symmetry. This method converges linearly, ensuring that the sequence of approximations becomes indefinitely close to the target value. We have proof for the convergence and an analysis of the rate of convergence. Our algorithm is applicable to a broad range of data sets that do not necessarily meet the standard requirement of having a mean value. We also explored properties of a related algorithm that splits a larger problem into several smaller subproblems, specifically convergence to a set of target values. Our method is relevant to fields that utilize and further develop L1-PCA, such as image denoising, deblurring, and compressive sensing.

This study proposes a method that employs BERT to enhance the tagging adjustment of questions linked to emotions, with the ultimate goal of creating engaging storytelling content. After analyzing research findings and BERT's structure, our approach involves three stages to refine labels based on BERT's output and narrative data. Specifically, it utilizes BERT to generate a semantic analysis of stories, identifies underrepresented tags in the BERT output, and adjusts the labeling of emotional questions by considering both the semantic meaning and statistical distribution of tags. When applied to the Task 1 of CCF 2021's Emotion-Connected Question Answering Challenge, our results show a notable improvement in accuracy rates.

This study introduces an innovative method of playing Power Games on subsets of a specific type of mathematical structure called the completely ordered groups. We prove that Power Games have fixed points within this specific type of structure when the groups in question are finite in size, and we also establish that the fixed points are unique. We further demonstrate that in the case of infinite groups, Power Games may not always result in fixed points. This study provides the theoretical basis for exploring a broader class of Power Games, including those played on sets of integers and rational numbers.

The theoretical model of asynchronous polars is tested against its non-synchronous counterpart using X-ray observations. By analyzing a sample of 13 asynchronous polars and 11 non-synchronous magnetic binaries with white dwarfs, we collected hardness ratios and spectral indices from the ROSAT all-sky survey, XMM-Newton, and Chandra, and computed their correlations. The data showed a positive correlation between hardness ratios and the temperature of the accretion column, but it was disrupted by the non-synchronous polars. A distinct characteristic of the non-synchronous polars is their higher temperature than the asynchronous polars, which cannot be explained by the X-ray model. The temperature difference is associated with the X-ray ratio, and it implies that the non-synchronous polars have a higher luminosity in soft X-rays than the asynchronous polars. No correlation was found between the spectral index and the column density or the temperature of the accretion column. The non-synchronous polars have a higher column density than the asynchronous polars, which cannot be fully accounted for by the dust absorption. No link was found between the X-ray ratio and the orbital period, the mass accretion rate, or the magnetic field strength. The unique characteristics of the non-synchronous polars are consistent with their unique magnetic geometry, which may allow for accretion over the entire white dwarf surface.

This study employs a reduced basis method (RBM) to solve a specific mathematical problem. The problem in question involves the interaction of a fluid and two deformable structures within the fluid. Two main techniques are utilized in this investigation: a unified approach and a divided approach for handling the two structures. The unified approach treats the two structures as a single entity with shared characteristics. The divided approach, on the other hand, applies separate reduced basis methods to the two structures. The investigation compares the two techniques's efficiency with changing fluid and structure parameters.

When navigating unfamiliar settings, individuals heavily rely on environmental layouts to inform their movements. Although the HiTMap concept has been proposed to improve navigation using a topological diagram, there is a lack of concrete implementation details. This study introduces a tangible HiTMap representation, comprising spatial regions connected by directional connections, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a simulation test. The findings show that participants navigated more efficiently when utilizing the HiTMap representation than with an unstructured layout. Furthermore, a survey revealed that the HiTMap was perceived as more understandable and appealing than a conventional topological map. This research provides a theoretical framework for the benefits of HiTMap and validates its superiority over traditional navigation methods, but there are areas for improvement, particularly regarding dynamic HiTMap creation and potential cognitive biases in participant perspectives.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task, focused on identifying and categorizing offensive text within Twitter posts, used a combination of BERT and Support Vector Machines. BERT was employed in both a traditional and a reduced form across tasks, with the aim of detecting hate speech. The evaluation revealed that the traditional BERT method rated the highest in accuracy, achieving 75.89% in macro F1 measure, while the reduced BERT method performed below average. Furthermore, combining BERT with linear kernel SVMs resulted in enhanced performance, particularly for the subspace approach, which utilized 75 features out of 680, and successfully detected 76.11% of offensive tweets.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring extremely small changes in magnetic fields. We propose an innovative approach to achieve this feat through atomic interferometry by leveraging the Meissner effect in superconductors. A superconducting film's ability to generate a gradient of static magnetic field can be utilized to enhance atomic interference visibility. This method allows for the sensitive measurement of local magnetic field alterations, potentially surpassing the limitations of other techniques. We examine the possibilities and constraints of this method, including sources of error and potential applications. Furthermore, we outline the requirements and advantages of using this method with atomic sensors that combine superconducting sensors and interferometric atoms. We also explore the scope for further improvement by considering technical limitations and potential alternatives to using superconducting films.

We investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of doped XTe (X=Na, K) monolayers using the first principles method and find that they develop magnetic characteristics due to close packing, which can be controlled through layer thickness. The results show that, despite varying chemical potential, the band structure remains magnetically stable within a certain range. The model demonstrates the emergence of magnetic transitions with chemical potential changes, a feature not commonly found in conventional magnetic materials. The model also exhibits unique characteristics where magnetic transitions can be induced by varying chemical potential, exchange coupling, or layer thickness. The findings indicate that transition metal dichalcogenides have the potential to display complex magnetic phenomena under close packing conditions.

We investigate how the electron-gravity field interaction affects light propagation within a gapped material, specifically in the gapped region near a surface. Our analysis considers two situations: one where the distance between two surfaces is significant and one where it's minimal. For the larger distance scenario, our findings align with previous research indicating that the electron-gravity field interaction doesn't significantly impact light propagation in this region. However, in the smaller distance scenario, our results reveal that the electron-gravity field interaction causes light propagation to slow down due to two factors: the redirection of electrons out of the surface region and the influence of electron motion on the electromagnetic field. This slowing effect is more pronounced when the distance between two surfaces is minimal.

Type theory's normalization properties are fundamental in ensuring the denotation of terms are well-defined. This research extends the normalizing properties to a higher degree of robustness, referred to as 'robust normalization,' which also has implications for the convergence of types. The effort results in a more stable type theory that maintains key properties of the Curry-Howard isomorphism, including the combination of modality and computation for propositional identity types.

The study of topological quantum phenomena is highly dependent on understanding the relationships between their hallmark features, such as gapless modes, interaction, and entanglement measures, especially in one-dimensional systems. By examining the symmetric tight-binding model, we gain insights into these concepts and their connections, both individually and collectively, in a topological phase. For example, we show that in the SSH model, focal point defects can be separated from each other based on both the energy spectra and the eigenfunction patterns, and that these points represent locations of singular interaction in momentum space. We also found that in the bulk phase, there is a direct correlation between the distance between these points and both the spatial separation of edge mode states and a measure of spatial entanglement. When the system is divided into two segments, we observe that a topological non-trivial phase can host a mobile, zero-energy mode that appears in one segment and a localized mode that appears in the other segment. We found that in the SSH model, the distance between these points can be adjusted by changing the spatial separation of the mode states, and that this distance is correlated with a measure of spatial entanglement. This understanding is also applicable to other one-dimensional models, and provides a foundation for exploring more complex systems.

Finite mixture models are examined in a more general framework that integrates elements from stochastic geometry and Choquet theory. This framework offers an enhanced perspective on mixture models, allowing their application to be broadened across multiple contexts. Furthermore, it provides a basis for exploring new types of mixture models.

We derive a two-loop amplitude formula for supergravity in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using an extension of the CTT (color-ordered, massless, two-loop) bootstrap method, tailored for massless fields in a redefined AdS$_5$ coordinate space. The bootstrapped expression takes the form of an AdS$_5$ times S$^5$-inspired extension of the four-dimensional CHY amplitude, and reveals a previously unseen connection to a five-dimensional integral representation. By transforming back to the standard AdS$_5$ coordinate space, we recover a five-dimensional AdS$_5$ times S$^5$-inspired extension of the two-loop gravity amplitude in ten-dimensional type IIB supergravity, obtained independently via the six-dimensional CHY approach. This methodology is applicable over all massless states within the supergravity theory.

Concurrent object-based programming on GPUs is made more efficient and safe with the aid of a sophisticated memory allocator, but developing one that balances fast memory allocation with proper memory alignment and padding is a complex task.

We have developed DynaSOAr, a flexible and efficient concurrent memory allocator tailored for object-based programming on GPUs, which utilizes binary search to quickly handle memory requests.

As DynaSOAr is a dynamic allocator, it is capable of managing memory blocks of any size, unlike static allocators, which are, however, more efficient in terms of memory usage due to reduced overhead.

In our evaluation, DynaSOAr exhibited a significant improvement in memory allocation speed, outperforming other state-of-the-art concurrent allocators by a factor of up to 5.3, while also demonstrating a notable decrease in memory usage, a 1.3 to 2.4 times improvement, in our object-based application benchmarks for GPU computation.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the compressibility of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of the partial differential operators and the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A new theoretical approach has been presented that uses basic concepts from quantum mechanics and electrodynamics to explain the spin polarization of localized states. This approach is then applied to analyze the experimental findings of YMoto et al. which involved the measurement of superconducting gap energies and magnetic susceptibility around the adatom and dipolar impurities using highly sensitive tunnel spectroscopy. The theoretical framework successfully explains the observed gap energy patterns and varying magnetic susceptibility in a way that is relevant to the manipulation of quasiparticle states.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates Fourier Series with Implicit Neural Representations to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier Morphable Grid (FMG) to define a function that predicts the intensity of pixels within a target object, allowing for flexible representation of geometric variations. During training, a Fourier target mask is generated for each object instance at each iteration, making it possible to apply instance-specific losses across all pixels. Our approach surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods in the MISC dataset, a challenging benchmark, and demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on the COCO dataset, while achieving this result without using bounding boxes or global instance masks.

This study examines how the range of an immersion that is bounded by a compact surface in three-dimensional space is determined, specifically focusing on the effects of negative curvature within that surface. We establish a critical volume threshold, directly influenced by the surface's Gaussian curvature, below which the immersed range does not fully encompass the bounded three-dimensional space. Moreover, when the bounded space has negatively curved walls, the immersed range occupies a significantly larger volume than the bounded space itself. This research also reveals that the same set of curves can be both locally and globally minimized in terms of the enclosed volume, demonstrating an unusual minimization problem in mathematics.

The formation of large, circular features in cloud fields is influenced by an underlying mechanism, likely caused by the interaction between updrafts and the distribution of cloud condensation nuclei.  Convective clouds, particularly those with heights over 6 km, offer a critical opportunity to study this relationship due to the condensation process's significant impact on cloud development.  Analyzing these clouds with high-resolution imaging from space can provide insights into their structure, however, their opacity hinders such analysis.  Recent studies have shown potential methods for deriving cloud imaging from space using data from the MODIS and MISR satellites.  This study proposes an enhanced approach using two types of veiled-core patterns, identified in imaging data, as a standard for cloud imaging.  The approach, validated through the comparison of imaging-derived parameters with existing measurements, shows a strong correlation and minimal scatter.  The study finds that the new approach yields a wider range of values than previous methods, potentially due to the inclusion of more robust data from the full MISR ensemble of images.  The proposed approach provides a standardized way to determine the central core of these clouds, allowing for the comparison of results from different studies and the exploration of relationships between cloud processes and large-scale weather patterns.

Our investigation offers a novel approach to enhance the efficiency of ion thrusters using a specific electromagnetic field configuration. We propose creating a field with negative permittivity and zero magnetic field that interacts with a pulsed, high-intensity laser beam in a highly diamagnetic plasma environment. When this interaction reaches a certain point, a rare phenomenon occurs, making the thruster's surrounding plasma 'transparent' to the electromagnetic field. We discovered that this 'transparency' effect can significantly reduce the amount of energy needed from the ion thruster by minimizing energy loss through electromagnetic field fluctuations. As a result, this reduction in energy loss can increase the final speed of ions by as much as fifty times, exceeding one hundred thousand meters per second. Consequently, the overall efficiency of the ion thruster is increased to a point where it is no longer limited by the speed of light in the local electromagnetic field, also known as the'speed of light in a vacuum'. We further found that this 'transparency' effect can be achieved by aligning the frequency of the laser beam with a specific range that is determined by the thruster's plasma environment. Once the 'transparency' effect is achieved, the ion thruster can operate in a more efficient manner even with a low-energy laser beam, also known as 'low-intensity', also resulting in a significant increase in the final speed of ions. We also found that this 'low-intensity' condition can lead to a significant increase in the final speed of ions by

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we present the TOI-712 multi-planetary system found in the saturated zone of $TESS$ data. By utilizing $SPITZER$ and $HUBBWi$, we determined the planetary sizes and estimated the orbital paths. The results show two mini-Neptunes, TOI-712 b and TOI-712 c, with sizes of approximately 28.964 $R_ \earth$ and 26.681 $R_ \earth$, and radii that are likely inflated by 10.3 $R_ \earth$ and 8.7 $R_ \earth$ in their orbits respectively. Furthermore, we discovered that TOI-712 d, the third planet in the system, has a highly eccentric orbit and falls within the livable zone with a size of about 22.807 $R_ \earth$. The moderately close proximity of the three planets in the system, with orbits of 2.504, 4.039, and 9.513 days, raises the likelihood of planetary interactions which could result in tidal forces and eventual loss of planetary mass over time.

This study examines the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To achieve this, we employed a slab model utilizing DFT calculations, with arrangements mimicking a (11$\bar{2}$0) surface of rutile TiO2.  A 2x2 supercell construction allowed us to study the effects of nitrogen and carbon defects at interstitial sites, along with substitutions for O atoms, by comparing their ground states.  Our calculations indicate that interstitial carbon and nitrogen defects tend to form p-states near the valence band maximum, resulting in nonmagnetic ground states.  Conversely, substitutions of C and N for O atoms yield magnetic ground states, with C impurities exhibiting one electron and N impurities exhibiting two electrons in their respective p-states.  This distinction arises due to the availability of electrons from the Ti d-states in the Ti-O-C/N arrangements.  Moreover, N and C defects can significantly alter the electronic structure, transforming TiO2 from an n-aeroelectric material to a ferroelectric or antiferroelectric material, depending on the site occupation.  Our findings are consistent with experimental outcomes, particularly in regards to the variation of binding energies observed in XPS spectra, which can be interpreted to infer the presence of C and N defects responsible for modifying the electronic and magnetic properties of TiO2.

The Current LHC energy facilitates the creation of pairs of heavy flavoured particles, specifically top quarks, through gluon interactions, yet their individual creation via elastic scattering of two high-energy particles remains undetected. This study suggests that observing the pair of heavy flavoured particles produced through the scattering of two high-energy particles, known as elastic production, can provide valuable insights into the properties of the fundamental interaction responsible for the creation of these particles. Furthermore, it highlights that even if pair production through the exchange of virtual particles is observed, knowing the properties of the interaction responsible for elastic production can providecomplementary information, which can be as significant as the data from pair production, thus warranting an exploration of this process at the LHC. This study also offers an innovative approach to identify the elusive process of individual heavy flavoured particle creation and highlights that, in certain scenarios, the observation of the pair of heavy flavoured particles produced through the scattering of two high-energy particles can provide valuable information on the properties of the fundamental interaction responsible for the creation of these particles.

Previous research analyzing the characteristics of the intra-cluster gas atmosphere, specifically the scaling properties of magnetic field fluctuations, encountered difficulties in determining the underlying causes of deviations from expected power laws. The current study assesses potential errors in measuring the structure functions of these fluctuations and confirms that they originate from a combination of observational limitations and statistical anomalies. The analysis suggests that the deviations arise primarily from the loss of detailed information due to the projection of three-dimensional observations in the plane of the sky. The results indicate that more sensitive radio observations, with a higher spatial resolution, are necessary to accurately understand the properties of intra-cluster gas atmospheres.

In this paper, we establish various Ramsey properties for specific subgraphs within infinite graph families that satisfy certain conditions. Specifically, we prove the existence of a high-density $K_{n}$ subgraph within infinite graph families consisting of graph products, planar graph families, and minimal graph embeddings, among others. To achieve this, we develop strategies for identifying desired subgraphs by applying graph preservation techniques and utilizing graph embedding theories. Furthermore, we investigate the minimum density required for an infinite graph family to contain a high-density $K_{n}$ subgraph that is connected to a specific component. The minimum density in question may be viewed as a topological version of Ramsey theory.

Located in the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a ring-like structure composed of molecular gas that is crucial for understanding how the galaxy's center evolved. To determine the mass distribution within this area, researchers typically utilize mapping techniques such as the Gimmick method and the Axisymowic Two-Dimensional Correlation method. Recently, a team of scientists discovered a previously hidden ring in the CMZ by employing the 13CS molecule mapping technique and analyzed their data using both methods, with the 2D Correlation method revealing a more accurate mass arrangement that is anisotropic in shape, similar to a distorted ellipse with 5.2 parsecs in length and 3.3 parsecs in width. By comparing their findings to existing studies, the mass distribution in the CMZ was estimated at approximately 8.7 x 10^3 solar masses, with a total mass ranging from 1.8 x 10^11 to 2.6 x 10^11 solar masses. Using a simplified model, the mass of individual objects within the ring was calculated, with the greatest mass concentrated in a cloud at the CMZ's 320 degree position, followed by the Giant Molecular Association and the 13CS ring's largest molecule gas mass. Additionally, a super massive black hole mass of 6.5 x 10^6 solar masses was confirmed through a common motion analysis of the 13CS ring, with further research needed to determine

This experiment uses artificial intelligence trained on video data to analyze eye movements, specifically on how they relate to Bell's Palsy symptoms. We observed a noticeable difference in eye motion patterns when patients with Bell's Palsy looked at their own reflection versus other people's reflections. This difference wasn't evident when healthy participants performed the same task. By studying eye movements in this context, we believe it may be possible to accurately identify Bell's Palsy in real-time using only visual data. To test this hypothesis, we trained an additional AI model on the data, which demonstrated a high success rate in predicting the presence of Bell's Palsy based on the associated eye movements.

The Quantum Double Quantum Computer is capable of executing quantum circuits from lattice gauge theories, offering a promising avenue for the study of quantum field theory using quantum simulation. In this paper, we explore the application of this system to the symmetric phase of quantum electrodynamics by utilizing qutrits to enhance the simulation of the electromagnetic field. We provide an expanded quantum circuit for the qutrits, detailing a quantum simulation that involves interacting finitely with matter fields on a spatial lattice while maintaining the freedom of massless photons. This paradigm includes an improved photoelectric effect and enables the creation of quantum states of electromagnetic fields via electromagnetic reactions. Furthermore, in the context of quantum simulation, we examine the photoelectric effect in relation to the reaction of an electron with qutrit mass and observe the emergence of continuous sound modes within the quantum simulation, closely resembling those of the electromagnetic field's infinite-depth, continuous mode spectrum.

The proposed future FLASHFORWARD experiment aims to achieve exceptionally high levels of polarization in electron beams by utilizing thick polarized positron sources. To reach these levels, researchers are collaborating to design a sophisticated positron source based on laser-illuminated thin foil targets. Under the influence of intense laser radiation, the positron source's polarization can reach nearly full utilization, with positrons emerging highly polarized even as they exit the target. Despite initial concerns that positron polarization could be limited by the target's thickness, simulations indicate that when placed within the range of the positron focus, a surprisingly small depth of around 0.5 millimeters is sufficient to produce highly polarized positrons. Furthermore, simulations suggest that this source could provide a significant amount of polarized power, with estimates suggesting up to 100 GW of highly polarized power could be achieved. To realize the full potential of this source, researchers are also exploring the properties of electron spectra and positron polarization as a function of angle, as well as the potential for bremsstrahlung radiation to impact the source's performance.

This study examines the underlying principles of groups of finite size that exhibit polynomial behavior under the operation of greatest common divisors. Specifically, it investigates the relationship between the degree of this polynomial behavior and the specific elements within the group. Furthermore, this analysis is expanded across multiple dimensions using a multi-variate approach, resulting in a deeper understanding of the group's structure and its relation to the degree of the polynomial behavior. This newfound insight can be applied to address prior questions concerning the existence of certain subsets within these groups.

This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensing chip capable of measuring local temperatures around the analog and digital components of a system, even in the presence of varying supply voltages and thermal zones. The design utilizes a precise temperature-dependent voltage difference between two parallel transistors, which is accurately calculated using a threshold voltage calculator and a digital temperature detector. The circuit can operate across a wide temperature range, from -40°C to 150°C, and has a high precision of 0.24°C. Furthermore, it can handle changing supply voltages ranging from 0.6V to 1.8V. The design's versatility allows it to be suitable for use in small IoT devices, wearable electronics, and large data center systems. However, it has a significant drawback of only being able to detect temperatures out of a pre-calibrated range, which means it may not accurately measure extremely low or high temperatures. This issue arises because the design relies on a limited set of measurement data during its development.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of stars, particularly in Ap-stars and White Dwarfs, has been a subject of extensive debate. The most widely accepted theory attributes its origin to extreme stability in the star's core, maintaining the axial symmetry of the magnetic field under any minor disturbances. The critical limit for this stability, as defined by the magnetic pressure over gas pressure, is five, which some studies have found within the range of 5-600 in these stars. However, the condition for spectral line observations, namely that the magnetic energy should exceed the kinetic energy, is not met in many instances. The accuracy of the tale of stable stellar cores relies on the results of a new analytical solution for marginal stability, which is obtained through a linearized approach in the presence of adiabatic equations. The solution shows that the ideal condition of marginal stability, if met exactly, would necessitate the equivalence of radial and horizontal perturbation pressures, a requirement that is not met in any of the observed Ap-stars and White Dwarfs. Consequently, the condition for perfect stability can be met only partially, if at all, and hence the tale of the stable stellar cores should be considered as an oversimplification.

Using the functional renormalization group (FRG), our study calculates precise fluid dynamics for the $O(N)$ model in zero-dimensional quantum field theory by solving a set of partial differential equations derived from the FRG approach. We verify the renormalization group flow equations for the $O(N)$ model in zero-dimensional quantum field theory, solving them analytically for both the Schwartz model and the $\phi^3$ theory. We validate the renormalization group flow equations for the $\phi^4$ theory through numerical methods. For all cases, our findings match established results obtained through other methods, providing a crucial check for the validity of our approach. Additionally, this work paves the way for extending the FRG method to more complex scenarios, including field theories in higher dimensions and near phase transition thresholds.

Music datasets pose a significant challenge to search due to their diverse nature. Existing search methods are often flawed as they rely heavily on frequency-based approaches, making them prone to biases. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel, meta-query-based method called Pied Piper, which incorporates multiple aspects of a dataset to conduct a more comprehensive search. By utilizing multiple patterns to rank results, Pied Piper helps reduce the emphasis on overrepresented items. Our method excels in particularity-oriented music retrieval tasks, as demonstrated through search experiments on various datasets. The code and dataset used in this study are publicly available for download.

This study establishes a precise link between geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and stacks by identifying the concrete symplectic manifolds that correspond to algebraic data derived from the structure of a Lie groupoid. Specifically, it demonstrates that a smooth configuration on a Lie groupoid is equivalent to a grassmannian bundle with structure group GL(+), and conversely, that a grassmannian bundle with this structure yields a smooth configuration on the associated stack. This connection provides a clear understanding of when two such configurations are equivalent. The research also shows that the space of linear configurations on a Lie groupoid is isomorphic to the space of representations of the groupoid's unit space, a fact with implications for the theory's symmetry.

Observations of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, conducted at 1.3 mm and 350 $\mu$m using the SHARK and HOBYS key projects of ATLASGAL, revealed a molecular core size that is greater than the millimeter continuum source size. This difference in sizes may indicate the presence of an expanding molecular core, with an estimated age of approximately 1.5 million years. If this hypothesis is correct, it suggests that the time required for a one-solar-mass protostar to reach 50 percent of its luminosity could be around 4-5 million years, thus providing a possible pathway for the formation of massive stars. In addition, this could imply that the time needed to break through a nearby O-type star's radiation field could be within 5-6.5 million years, thus offering a potential solution to the problem of massive star formation over large distances.

This research paper proposes an equal accessibility relation R for the Godel modal logic to operate on top of, such that it behaves similarly to standard modal logic. Godel modal logic can be seen as an expansion of classical modal logic using prelinearity, distributing infinitary disjunction and the rule of congruence for counterfactuals. Our proposed relation R encompasses various other extensions of Godel modal logic, including those over finite algebras with series reduct, certain finite relational structures, and certain infinite algebras.

LiDAR systems are widely utilized for safe and efficient road network mapping by automating the collection of 3D point data. These datasets contain numerous critical information points, including road markings, curbs, and operational intersections, which are essential for advanced driver-assistance systems and autonomous vehicle navigation. Although significant progress has been made in leveraging LiDAR data for spatial awareness, there is still a significant challenge in beign able to extract relevant information from these 3D point sets to support CCAV systems. With the emergence of new 3D feature learning techniques, it is now possible to extract contextual and hierarchical 3D descriptors from LiDAR data, but it remains to be seen whether these methods can effectively tackle the practitioners' problems of extracting critical information from these datasets. With the high costs associated with collecting and labeling large LiDAR datasets, it is also unclear whether existing methods can be robust to variations in LiDAR data when tested on smaller datasets. This work aims to address these uncertainties by evaluating the current state-of-the-art 3D LiDAR learning techniques on a newly collected and extensively annotated dataset containing critical information points, and also testing their performance under real-world LiDAR data collection conditions. With the future direction of LiDAR-based 3D learning towards extracting information from these datasets becoming increasingly dependent on the outcomes of this research, it is essential to share the findings with the community. This study investigates whether certain characteristics of spherical stochastic processes remain the same at any given point, and finds that an important condition is a relationship involving the harmonic analysis coefficients of the process. We demonstrate this condition ensures that the process has the same mean and variance at any point on the sphere. The article also explores a simpler condition for Gaussian processes to have stationary increments on the sphere.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles, primarily neutrinos, remains unknown despite significant research efforts. Neutrinos offer a key clue in this mystery, as they are produced by massive astrophysical events involving high-energy processes, such as supernovae or the accretion of material into black holes. To uncover the connections between neutrinos and other cosmic particles, we analyzed three years of data from the IceCube Neutrino Telescope in search of links between neutrino flux and the arrival directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles. This study reveals a significant correlation between the two, with a p-value of 0.035, and the excess of particle arrivals from high-neutrino-flux directions is estimated at 4.5±2.1 per cent. While this association is statistically significant, further investigation is needed to determine its significance in the context of the overall excess of ultra-high-energy particle arrivals, which was previously reported.

The flow resistance of liquid foams is heavily influenced by two opposing forces: the restrictive nature of the interconnected solid structures and the irregularities in the surface. This study focuses on the impact of surface irregularities on flow resistance. It's observed that as the viscosity of the liquid increases, the surface irregularities have a more significant effect on flow resistance. This influence can be explained by a relationship that takes into consideration the ratio of the liquid's viscosity to the strength of the foam structures and remains consistent across various scales of measurement. Moreover, this relationship can be applied to control the flow of foams with complex surfaces over rough substrates, predicting that the flow will become more turbulent as the ratio of viscosity to structural strength increases, eventually shifting to laminar flow when the surface irregularities are minimized.

Building on conventional support vector machine technology, we explored the use of a unique approach that incorporates local descriptors and abnormal sample elimination techniques in our research. Specifically, we combined textural features extracted via local binary pattern and gray level co-occurrence matrix methods, and employed a deep learning architecture known as the recurrent attention deep learning network to identify outliers among histopathological images of skin carcinomas. Compared to standard approaches, our method yielded superior results in classifying tumor types and detecting anomalous images, with an overall accuracy of 92.9%. Notably, our method's ability to identify irregularities among training and validation datasets significantly improved prediction efficacy.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a suspended layer over an increasingly permeable substrate reveals a critical point at moderate rotation speeds, characterized by a sudden and persistent shift from orderly patterns to chaotic ones. The normally stable fingers that form in this context can suddenly shift to an unstable configuration, with multiple narrow bands forming in the process. This degree of flexibility is unique to this specific combination of forces and constraints, making it an intriguing phenomenon that sets this particular system of fluids apart.

In contrast to traditional theories, classical Hamiltonian dynamics is uniquely characterized by its stable fixed point at the equilibrium state, which represents a perfect balance where no macroscopic flow occurs. This exceptional feature gives rise to an intriguing paradox - since the phase space volume remains constant, initial conditions can be precisely predicted from final observations, which is an ideal situation but only feasible in theory. Unfortunately, this wonderful outlook is marred by the unsettling presence of singularities, which create unresolvable determinism issues. The unconstrained expansion model attempts to break free from these constraints by introducing an infinite set of Hamiltonian flow equations, which are solved using an innovative method that circumvents the difficulty of volume alteration. This solution employs a novel approach to eliminate the large ratio of time scales, leveraging the diverse frequencies of molecular vibrations, rotations, and vibrations to create a hierarchical framework of Hamiltonian pathways. This expansion strategy holds the promise of generating precise, coherent spectra from first principles, a feat considered impossible by current standards.

Two specific variations of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, namely chlorinated CCH and CN forms, have been previously undetected in TMC-1. To differentiate between the two, we employed GALS to determine the relative abundances of the two ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers. By utilizing the values of column densities and correcting for the fraction of incident radiation, we calculated the total amount of ethynyl cyclopadiene in TMC-1. The results indicate that both the CCH and CN forms have abundant quantities, with the CCH form being roughly twice as common as the CN form. The relative abundance of the two variations varies based on the specific line used for identification, with an average ratio ranging between 1.5:1 and 2.5:1 in favor of the CCH form. The overall amount of ethynyl cyclopentadiene in TMC-1 is found to be approximately 1.4 10^7 cm^-2. The discovery of these two variations of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, specifically the CCH form with a five-membered ring, provides the first observational evidence for a cyclopentadiene molecule linked to a chlorine atom, contributing to our understanding of the chemical processes occurring in molecular clouds.

Current neural machine translation models excel at generating precise sequences of words, but they often struggle to produce accurate sentences. This issue is compounded when these systems are paired with a sentence-focused attention mechanism, as seen in neural machine translation models using extended attention. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, modified attention mechanism that incorporates a look-ahead focus on the target language. By doing so, we enable the attention mechanism to consider both the source sentence and the desired output sentence. This look-ahead focus on the target sentence is equivalent to a focus on the source sentence that takes into account the output sequence. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, referred to as creation attention, by integrating it into a neural machine translation model. Our evaluation reveals that creation attention yields a significant improvement in BLEU scores when compared to a widely-used state-of-the-art neural machine translation model, including both a baseline model and one featuring extended attention.

The success of software development methods depends on their ability to balance practicality and effectiveness. While some methods are highly research-active, others are more focused on delivering working software through collaboration. Our experience developing the GridFlow approach and the Gridware framework reveals the value of a translational method that divides the development process into manageable stages, providing both design principles and implementation guidance. By doing so, developers can leverage existing design patterns to address problems, thereby preventing implementation issues. We demonstrate that this method's emphasis on incremental progress and continuous refinement leads to better software performance. Furthermore, we believe that other software development communities can benefit from adopting this approach.

A new cosmological model is presented, based on a combined dark substance model, which incorporates features of quintessence and dark matter. The model's fundamental equation is derived, and subsequently, the Hubble parameter's expression is obtained. By applying the Bandler method, the model's critical cosmological parameter is determined for various data sets, and subsequent predictions for the model's behavior in various epochs are made. Furthermore, the model exhibits distinct evolution paths compared to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, particularly in the early stages of the universe. The model's propensity for generating primordial perturbations is explored, and the derived expression for the density fluctuation amplitude is determined, satisfying the primordial fluctuation requirement of $10^{-5}$.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for the future workforce's needs.  Unfortunately, many school systems inadvertently undermine curiosity by focusing on test-taking strategies.  Teachers need tools that measure curiosity dynamically, but current methods are too restrictive.  To address this gap, we developed an innovative theoretical framework that combines economics, learning theories, and social influence models to create a computational curiosity model.  To test this framework's efficacy, we designed a computer-based simulation of a learning environment involving economics, a variant of the Ultimatum Game, and a discussion forum.  Participants' keyboard activity, screen interactions, and discussion forum content were analyzed to assess the curiosity model's performance.  Our results showed that the proposed method effectively measured children's curiosity, a correlation between high-curiosity children and fair-minded decision-making, and distinct patterns in keyboard and screen interactions that differentiated high and low curiosity groups.  Additionally, our study revealed that children's curiosity is associated with fair social behavior and is influenced by the learning environment.  These findings have implications for the design of technology-enhanced learning tools that can provide real-time, multi-modal curiosity indicators, enabling more effective support and promotion of curiosity.  Our proposed method can be applied to explore the complex dynamics of curiosity in various learning contexts.

This study introduces a novel set of functions, centered on a specific Mat\'ern parameter $\nu$, which are elements of a Gaussian process and excel at adapting to complex data patterns across various functions, including polynomial, exponential, and power-law curves, with specific values of $\nu$ yielding well-known functions like the squared exponential and Wiener kernel.

The optimal method for detecting road types in an urban area using a ridesharing vehicle's navigation system is an important problem to solve. By analyzing trip data, we can derive a detection protocol that minimizes cost by determining the most efficient road to detect based on its length and characteristics. However, the protocol's effectiveness depends on factors like the accuracy of the vehicle's sensor and navigation system. By assuming a perfect system, we can develop an approach to optimize the protocol, but real-world issues like false readings and system errors need to be addressed in future research.

A comprehensive statistical framework, efficient field theory, provides a thorough analysis of the consequences of an anomalous $J/\psi$ decay pattern, specifically focusing on the process $J/\psi\to \gamma + \text{invisible}$. To achieve this, the decay into a subeath-energy photon and a dark energy particle or a pair of neutrino photons is considered, with the constraint that the photon's energy exceeds 100 MeV. Employing a global fit approach, the model's parameters are determined using experimental data from various $J/\psi$ decay experiments, with the option to include an anomalous contribution. The results indicate that for a 10 femtobarn $-1$ year of luminosity in $e+e-$ collisions, the sensitivity to a specific parameter value can be quite high, with a range of $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-5}$, covering a vast range of current theoretical predictions. Additionally, the study finds that for a particular efficient field theory scenario, a substantial fraction of the parameter space will be ruled out by experiments in the future, with the possibility of confirming or disproving the model through future experiments.

The variable timestep version of the recently introduced Second Derivative Implicit MultiStep Integration Method has been developed, and its properties including convergence and consistency have been proven. This new method can be applied to solve ordinary and partial differential equations using a range step that can vary in size. 

In the case of partial differential equations, the method involves converting the partial differential equation into a system of ordinary differential equations via spatial discretization. The variable timestep method for these equations yields a solution that is accurate up to the second order of convergence, in both time step size and local truncation error. 

The method can be implemented using a timestepping strategy that controls the time step size based on the solution's characteristics, and it results in a more efficient algorithm when compared to a fixed timestep method. The method's properties, including stability and a bounded solution, are guaranteed for any reasonable choice of the timestepping control parameter. The method can be applied to solve a wide range of nonlinear differential equations, including those with varying coefficients and equations with stiff and nonstiff components.

This study introduces a multivariate functional singular spectrum evaluation (MFSE) approach, capable of analyzing high-dimensional data sets comprising multiple functional time series. The development of asymptotic theory for the proposed method's optimal parameter and associated convergence rates is a key area of focus. As part of the general theory, specific results on the optimal convergence rate of the MFSE estimator's risk have been derived, taking into account various dimensional configurations, including when the data sets share parameters, overlap in frequency, and exhibit non-stationarity. The efficiency of the MFSE approach is demonstrated through numerical examples and graphical visuals, showcasing its application across multivariate functional time series.

The fundamental concept of stability in optimization methods, as seen with the AES frameworks, is often misunderstoodly equated with the lack of sensitivity issue, which arises from the large step size. To address this, the paper examines the distinction between stability and sensitivity in AES frameworks through the lens of an optimal control problem. It identifies the underlying causes of both the stability and sensitivity problems, and suggests potential remedies, including the use of a stability-respecting step size, dynamic scheduling, and robust regularizers, that aim to enhance the efficacy of AES frameworks.

This study examines a one-dimensional random walk that, due to an unobservable local time interval, appears partially visible to the observer. We aim to determine the probability that the observed section meets specific conditions, finding that it equals $e^{-2\lambda x}(1-e^{-2\lambda(x-y)})^2$ for $y \leq x$, and $e^{-2\lambda x}(1-e^{-2\lambda(x-y)})^2 + e^{-2\lambda y}(1-e^{-2\lambda(x-y)})^2$ for $y > x$. These probabilities can be utilized to derive probabilities for more complex scenarios, including cases where the unobserved section meets particular conditions. We utilize these probabilities to investigate two scenarios: the first scenario involves a walk that must meet the condition $y+\sqrt{x-y}\lambda^{-1}u$ to continue, with $u$ being a uniform variable on $[0,1]$; the second scenario involves a walk that must meet the condition $\sqrt{x-y}\lambda^{-1}u$ to stop, with $u$ being a uniform variable on $[0,1]$.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is undergoing a transformation to meet new safety standards, which will result in a significant modification to its plasma chamber. A new plasma source, designed for helicon wave production, has been installed as part of these changes. To ensure accuracy, computer simulations were used to model the new plasma source, and their results were compared with actual measurements taken during recent experiments. Although some discrepancies were found, they were ultimately confirmed to be the result of measurement errors, and good agreement was found between the simulations and a previous study. The validated simulations can now be used to gain a deeper understanding of the plasma source's operation and will be instrumental in identifying areas that could benefit from improvement, such as the plasma source's narrow current distribution.

The model we've developed is an extension of a previous microbial pesticide model, which incorporates the active ingredient's suppressing effect on the host plant and resulting crop output. The modified model adds a new compartment representing the suppressive activity, while maintaining the original model's compartmental structure, except for the infected compartment which reaches a saturated equilibrium. This extended model yields a second stable equilibrium at a more optimal balance between infected and free bacteria, and reveals the counterintuitive consequence of increasing suppressive activity on the microbial population through its impact on crop output. However, this model is susceptible to instability caused by feedback loops, and controlling this instability is critical for developing optimal microbial pesticide strategies.

In precision medicine, identifying cancer cells through image analysis is a crucial step in treating patients and determining the best course of treatment.  However, accurately detecting these cells is extremely difficult and there is a lot of interest in using deep learning techniques to automate this process.  By transforming traditional image classification networks into inverse problems, researchers have made significant progress in this area, but these methods have a major limitation - they can only be applied to detect objects of a single class.  For example, detecting multiple nuclei in an image is equivalent to solving one instance of the binary integer programming problem, but this is not a problem that current techniques can solve effectively.  To address this limitation, we propose a novel new approach called W-Net, which uses two stages to solve this kind of inverse problem.  In this approach, a first stage uses a conventional classification network to estimate the presence or absence of a nucleus at a specific location, but does this for all possible locations in the image.  Then, in the second stage, we use the output of the first stage to construct an energy function that minimizes the number of nuclei in the image, which allows us to include the constraint that a nucleus must be present.  We evaluated our approach on a public dataset and the results show that it outperforms the state of the art methods.

This study proves the converse Iwasawa recursion for the groups of odd special orthogonal and symplectic types, specifically for their $p$-adic analogues, beyond the classical cases covered by the Cassetto-Clozel Theorems 1.3 and 1.4.

A graph G is considered to have an detectable hamiltonian property if a hamiltonian path in G can be deduced from a hamiltonian path in an iterated line graph of G. This paper examines specific instances of graphs that have detectable hamiltonian paths, particularly focusing on the concept of hamiltonian path index 2, which implies that an hamiltonian path in G can be derived from a hamiltonian path in an line graph of G. We introduce new classifications for graph families with hamiltonian path index 2, based on their connection to line graphs, and provide examples of graph families with detectable hamiltonian properties, even though they may not have the property themselves. Additionally, we establish new limitations and classifications for graph families with hamiltonian path index 2, including those related to graph size and the presence of particular subgraphs.

Cell death, specifically pyroptosis, which is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, leads to severe inflammation that contributes to life-threatening complications and ultimate death in patients.  Pyroptosis is characterized by the breakdown of cellular membranes leading to inflammation and neighboring cell damage.  Research has shown that increased inflammation, resulting from pyroptosis, can cause acute respiratory distress syndrome and other critical conditions in COVID-19 patients.  While the exact mechanisms of pyroptosis induced by the SARS-CoV-2 virus are not yet fully understood, recent findings suggest that it is linked to the virus's ability to evade the host's immune system by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which normally leads to pyroptosis.  This study presents a mathematical model that represents the dynamics of pyroptosis and the NLRP3 inflammasome, as well as the host's immune cells and the SARS-CoV-2 virus.  The model also accounts for the effects of anti-inflammatory treatments on pyroptosis and inflammation, and the results show that such treatments can reduce inflammation by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation, thus preventing cellular death and subsequent organ failure.  The study suggests that timely anti-inflammatory intervention can lead to better outcomes, including reduced mortality and complications in COVID-19 patients.

External observations and state variables are necessary for reinforcement learning agents interacting with complex environments, especially those based on relational tables. However, using these agents in scenarios where the underlying data isn't visible poses a significant challenge. This problem is addressed by a new method developed by researchers, which extracts the essential external information needed for optimal policy determination and eliminates unnecessary variables and cues. This approach is proven to yield an optimally efficient solution, and a companion algorithm is provided to put the method into practice. The researchers further demonstrate the effectiveness of their method by applying it to resolve a prominent issue in cooperative reinforcement learning. This involves resolving the challenge of learning from data that isn't fully observable, such as the absence of explicit data on fellow agent positions, which is a critical obstacle in collaborative tasks.

A blockchain-based smart contract on Tezos, specifically on the Haskell implementation called HELM, is validated using a vendor-neutral inspection method based on refinement types. This approach, developed by the HELM project, offers a independent and language-agnostic verification procedure. As a result, the project has yielded a versatile refinement type system, called hlm2tex, capable of translating refinement types into the Michelson programming language used for Tezos smart contracts. This translation has been fully implemented in a validation tool called hlm2tex, which provides users with the capability to verify Tezos smart contracts written in HELM through type checking, as well as the ability to utilize external libraries and tools. Additionally, the project has introduced innovative features such as array and option refinement types, appraisals, and do-notation for simplifying the expression of refinements. The development of hlm2tex offers a promising pathway for the integration of refinement types and type checking in blockchain-based smart contracts.

Deep Neural Network methods, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, whereas traditional Neural Networks are constrained by their limited ability to handle such data. We investigated the underlying connection between GCNNs and conventional Neural Networks by applying a matched filtering approach, which reveals that GCNNs essentially use a form of spatial template matching to incorporate neighboring information. This understanding provides valuable insights into the operation of GCNNs, while also highlighting potential drawbacks related to limited angular resolution and ambigity. These findings are demonstrated through numerical examples and visualizations using a simple matched filtering network, which is then applied to solve an inverse problem in optics. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that GCNNs equate to matched filtering using nearby data points as templates, which facilitates a link between the network's learnable parameters and traditional inverse problems. By establishing this connection, we believe that leveraging expertise in inverse problems can boost the performance of GCNNs in image reconstruction tasks.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity can be represented using a Chern-Simons action for a connection that combines the Einstein-Algbert connection and a connection related to a scalar field. This paper explores the consequences of this approach, revealing that it yields spinning black holes and solitons with characteristics that can be described by gauge fields derived from vector multiplets. The solution takes the form of an extreme rotating black hole surrounded by an ergosphere, and it can also describe solitons with non-zero electric charge. The Chern-Simons term produces a conserved quantity, analogous to angular momentum in the Einstein-Hilbert action, enabling the solution of flat spacetime constrained by a loop. This loop constitutes the hairy black hole or soliton, and it remains unchanged over time due to the conservation of the associated charge. The approach can also handle multiple hairy black holes or solitons when they do not intersect, and it provides an equation that relates the electric charge to the loop's magnetic charge, as does the three-dimensional general relativity with gravitons and gravitinos.

We're investigating how branes maintain reversibility in a variety of contexts, from supergravity to conformal field theory, when the underlying spacetime symmetry is impaired. Some branes essentially maintain the symmetry that governs them, albeit in an impaired form, while others seek alternative pathways to achieve the same effect. This study sheds light on the branes' non-reversible behavior, revealing a direct connection between their altered trajectories and the resulting irregular patterns.

Precise calculation of tissue displacement is crucial for ultrasound elastography accuracy. The Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique enhances synthetic aperture ultrasound imaging to minimize errors in tissue displacement estimation. By mimicking the virtual source concept, VOSA reduces the systematic error associated with synthetic aperture imaging, which can impact the accuracy of elastography. We present a mathematical model representing the relationship between synthetic and virtual source-induced tissue displacements and derive corresponding cross-correlation functions to locate the maximum displacement. Furthermore, we propose a method to calculate the precise lateral shift of tissue displacement and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical analysis and experimental results, which show a significant improvement in the estimation of lateral shift.

Students learn programming concepts best through explicit connections between theoretical explanations and hands-on experiences, including both algorithmic descriptions and practical coding exercises. To strengthen these connections, we introduce a new approach to teaching programming concepts using "rational pseudocode," a graphical representation of fundamental principles. This approach focuses on abstracting technology details to highlight essential computational concepts. We've applied this method to create a comprehensive set of educational materials covering basic data structures and algorithms. These resources incorporate rational pseudocodes alongside step-by-step breakdowns of algorithm implementations in multiple programming languages. We've gathered empirical evidence to support the effectiveness of this method in improving student understanding of programming concepts through examples of student outcomes and instructor feedback. We believe our approach can be valuable for any educational initiative aiming to teach fundamental programming concepts.

Minic and Rossler introduced Boolean structures based on posets and variables, stating their Ramsey theorem for chains and antichains. This paper builds upon that work by proving a generalized Ramsey theorem applicable to V-shaped posets.

In the context of high-dimensional data, our study focuses on an adapted version of the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem, where we're working with a continuous stream of points with unknown or fixed labels. Our primary concern is minimizing the storage required to hold the centroid representatives of the clusters. We've developed a simplified storage approach that only holds the median of the current point's neighbors among the previous data set, and this has very brief overhead compared to the overall data size. Our main achievement is ensuring that with a fixed proportion of stored centroid representatives, our algorithm can recover the existing clusters and assign each new point to a cluster with a probability of at least $1-e^{-\Omega(d\epsilon^2)}$ if the data points have a fixed mean distance from each other and the clustering structure is robust enough. Additionally, we've established an lower bound to show that the storage requirement for an almost optimal dynamic $k$-means clustering algorithm increases with the number of data dimensions.

We introduce a new category of games that builds upon the foundation of stochastic repeated games, specifically Static Stochastic Games with Memory (SSGMs). SSGMs encompass a broad range of game types, including concurrent zero-sum games and correlated equilibria. We focus on a subset of SSGMs, which we call Hierarchical SSGMs (HSSGMs), characterized by players making independent decisions in distinct hierarchical layers. Our primary achievement lies in establishing a convertible format for HSSGMs, which allows us to apply linear programming to solve a broader class of near-Hierarchical SSGMs efficiently. We also explore the potential for self-organizing solutions within HSSGMs through the development of a decentralized learning algorithm. This research provides a groundwork for future investigations into the vast realm of SSGMs.

A nontransitive likelihood scenario occurs when there exists an experimental setup where data D generated by conducting experiment E yields the consequence that model M is likely to yield better results than model N, while data D, produced by conducting identical experiment E, also leads to the conclusion that model N is likely to yield better results than model O, yet data D, produced by conducting the same experiment E, results in the conclusion that model O is likely to yield better results than model N. We refer to any likelihood that gives rise to this situation as a nontransitive likelihood and demonstrate that it is equivalent to having the ability to select one parameter θ over another parameter φ based on a corresponding ability to select one circular order C over another circular order D, where the ability to choose θ over φ is equivalent to the ability to choose C over D if and only if the probability of observing data D, produced by conducting experiment E, is greater than the probability of observing data D, produced by conducting experiment E, for all possible data D. We then go on to prove that a likelihood will result in a nontransitive situation if and only if there exists a way to gamble on the basis of data D using a probability distribution p(·|D) that allows us to win a bet against a competitor who is using a probability distribution p(·|D') for some data sets D and D'.
